items.title: Developer runs public test where 2,000 people sent 6,000 emails trying to hack AI assistant; secrets.env file never leaked despite sophisticated prompt injection attempts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What happened after 2k people tried to hack my AI assistant
items.summary:
A developer created an AI assistant named Fiu and publicly invited over 2,000 people to try hacking it by sending more than 6,000 emails aimed at extracting the contents of a protected secrets.env file. Despite numerous sophisticated prompt injection attempts, including impersonation and multi-language social engineering, the AI successfully resisted all efforts and never leaked the sensitive information.

The experiment revealed that the AI, running on Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 model, effectively followed simple security instructions and identified coordinated attack patterns. Although the test incurred significant API costs and temporarily triggered fraud detection on the developer's email account, it demonstrated the model's robustness against prompt injection attacks and provided valuable insights into AI security vulnerabilities and defenses.

The developer concluded that while prompt injection remains a security concern, powerful models with proper safeguards can significantly mitigate risks. Future tests may involve weaker models and interactive responses to better understand the limits of AI security. The project also attracted sponsorship to support ongoing research and experimentation.

The new M7 series is expected to deliver significant performance improvements tailored for AI workloads, marking a departure from the traditional chip upgrade cycle. items.title: OpenKnowledge launches open source AI-first markdown editor and LLM wiki with integrations for Claude, Codex, and Cursor, available on macOS, Linux, and Windows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: OpenKnowledge – open source AI-first alternative to Obsidian/Notion
items.summary:
OpenKnowledge is a new open source, AI-first markdown editor and LLM wiki that integrates with AI models like Claude, Codex, and Cursor. It offers a local-first, full WYSIWYG editing experience similar to Google Docs or Notion, supporting collaborative AI-assisted editing and team sharing with automatic syncing via git and GitHub. The software is available as a macOS desktop app and as a web app or CLI tool for Linux, Windows, and Intel Mac systems.

The platform includes features such as agentic search, no-code team sharing, and support for multiple AI harnesses through its MCP/CLI interface. Users can install and run the editor locally, with documentation and contributions welcomed through its GitHub repository. OpenKnowledge is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later, emphasizing its open source nature and community-driven development.

items.title: Unconventional AI releases Un-0, an image generator using simulated coupled oscillators, achieving FID 6.74 on ImageNet 64×64 with open-source weights and code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Un-0: Generating Images with Coupled Oscillators
items.summary:
Unconventional AI has introduced Un-0, an image generator that uses a simulated system of coupled oscillators to create images. This approach, which leverages physical computing principles rather than traditional deep neural networks on GPUs, achieves a Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) score of 6.74 on the ImageNet 64×64 dataset, comparable to early leading image generation methods. The team has released the model weights, training code, and evaluation tools as open source to encourage further experimentation.

Un-0 operates by simulating thousands of coupled oscillators, each influencing the others through learned coupling strengths, inspired by natural synchronization phenomena like metronomes ticking in unison. This method represents a step toward more energy-efficient AI computing, potentially reducing energy consumption by up to 1,000 times compared to current hardware. The project builds on a history of physics-based computing models and aims to demonstrate that modern AI tasks can be effectively mapped onto physical dynamical systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce ContextForge for context recycling in long-horizon LLM inference, improving consistency and reducing token use in 15-turn healthcare query benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Context Recycling for Long-Horizon LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ContextForge, a system designed to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon conversational tasks by recycling context. ContextForge combines structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis to maintain relevant information across multiple turns without replaying the entire context, thereby reducing token usage while preserving answer quality. The system was tested on a 15-turn healthcare query benchmark, demonstrating improved consistency and reduced token consumption compared to baseline models, with comparable accuracy.

The evaluation focused on multi-turn reasoning, handling back-references, and adapting to domain shifts within structured healthcare queries. ContextForge's approach allows efficient reuse of prior computations, addressing limitations of context window size and token inefficiency in LLMs. This method offers a practical way to extend LLM capabilities for long conversations without needing larger context windows or retraining the models. The code and evaluation materials are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in short-context reasoning but degrade in performance over long conversational horizons due to context window limitations and inefficient token usage. We introduce ContextForge, a system for context recycling that maintains task-relevant information across turns by combining structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis. The system enables efficient reuse of prior computation without relying on full context replay, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. We evaluate ContextForge using a 15-turn conversational benchmark that tests multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts across structured healthcare queries. Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge demonstrates improved consistency and reduced token consumption, while maintaining comparable response accuracy. These results suggest that context recycling provides a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/Betanu701/ContextForge.

items.title: arXiv: Multimodal Large Language Models survey unified vision-language perception evolution with five-stage taxonomy and research roadmap toward general multimodal intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Structure to Synergy: A Survey of Vision-Language Perception Paradigm Evolution in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary:
A new survey on arXiv examines the evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that integrate vision and language into a unified perception capability. The study introduces a five-stage taxonomy to trace the development of these models, highlighting key methods and milestones that have advanced perception-centric intelligence. It also identifies challenges and proposes future research directions aimed at achieving general multimodal intelligence.

The survey addresses a gap in existing literature by treating vision and language as inseparable modalities, unlike prior reviews that often consider them separately. By formalizing MLLM perception as analogous to human innate perception, the authors provide a foundational framework and roadmap to guide further innovation toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently made remarkable progress in unifying vision-language understanding and reasoning, especially following the introduction of models such as OpenAI's O-series and DeepSeek's R-series, which have driven a paradigm shift toward perception-centric intelligence. However, there remains a lack of systematic surveys that examine perception from a truly unified vision-language perspective -- one that treats vision and language as an inseparable modality. Existing reviews are often fragmented, focusing separately on either vision or language, and thus rarely capture the cross-modal evolution of perception as an integrated capability. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic survey of unified vision-language perception in MLLMs. Specifically, we (1) formalize MLLM perception as an intrinsic, unified vision-language capability analogous to human innate perception, (2) introduce a five-stage taxonomy tracing the paradigm evolution of MLLM perception and survey representative methods and milestones at each phase, and (3) identify open challenges and outline promising research directions toward truly general, unified multimodal intelligence. We hope our study will provide both a foundational understanding and an actionable roadmap to foster further innovation on the path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

items.title: Researchers propose a dual-purpose framework using self-supervised Transformers and LLM-distilled taxonomies to improve cross-platform session embeddings for financial services recommendations, boosting recall and reducing loss [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a dual-purpose framework that leverages self-supervised Transformers and large language model (LLM)-distilled taxonomies to enhance cross-platform session embeddings for financial services recommendations. This approach addresses the challenge of integrating pre-login web interactions with authenticated in-app experiences, which traditionally differ and complicate user intent modeling. By converting raw web clickstreams into compact session embeddings and interpretable intent labels, the system improves recommendation accuracy and provides qualitative insights.

The framework demonstrates significant performance gains in production settings, including a 1.88% increase in macro Recall@1 and a 13.38% reduction in Log Loss for mobile homepage tile ranking tasks. Additionally, the session embeddings outperform LLM-generated labels by 4.3% on micro F1 in user conversion prediction, while the taxonomy distillation layer delivers interpretable labels with minimal latency and only a slight performance trade-off. This scalable solution offers a more flexible and effective method for capturing web-based user intent to enhance personalization in financial services.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

items.title: Researchers evaluate out-of-band defenses against prompt injection in LLM agents using adaptive attacks on AgentDojo, finding Progent reduces attack success from 25.8% to 4.2% on Qwen2.5-7B model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated out-of-band defenses against prompt injection attacks in large language model (LLM) agents, focusing on systems like Progent that enforce security policies outside the model rather than relying on in-model refusals. Their study applied an adaptive attack protocol on the AgentDojo benchmark using the Qwen2.5-7B model, finding that Progent reduced the average attack success rate from 25.8% to 4.2%, demonstrating resilience against adaptive, defense-aware attacks.

The research organizes these defenses within classical security frameworks such as integrity protection and reference monitoring, highlighting that prior validations relied on static benchmarks vulnerable to adaptive attacks. By independently reproducing and extending Progent's adaptive-attack analysis in a new setting, the study confirms the effectiveness of deterministic out-of-band enforcement, though it notes that stronger white-box attacks remain untested.

These findings suggest that out-of-band security measures may present a more robust barrier to adaptive prompt injection than in-band detection methods, offering a promising direction for securing tool-using LLM agents against sophisticated adversarial inputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work (2024 to 2026) has converged on a strategy for defending tool-using LLM agents against indirect prompt injection: rather than training the model to refuse malicious instructions, enforce security outside the model with a deterministic policy that mediates the agent's actions. Systems such as CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE realize this with capabilities, information-flow labels, and reference monitors, and several report near-elimination of attacks on the AgentDojo benchmark. We make two contributions. First, we organize these out-of-band defenses as instances of classical integrity protection (Biba), reference monitoring, and least privilege, yielding a structured comparison of what they do and do not cover. Second, we warn that every one of them is validated only on static benchmarks (a fixed set of injection attempts), the same methodology that made in-band defenses look strong until adaptive, defense-aware attacks broke twelve of them at over 90% success; we specify the threat model and protocol an adaptive evaluation requires. We then run that protocol as an independent reproduction and extension of Progent's own adaptive-attack analysis, on AgentDojo, with an open-weight agent (Qwen2.5-7B) self-hosted on a single H200, a setting its authors did not test. Averaged over three runs, the defense held: Progent cut mean attack success roughly sixfold (25.8% to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%). This is one small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box attack template; a stronger optimized (white-box GCG) attack remains open. The result is consistent with, but does not establish, the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is a harder target for an adaptive attacker than in-band detection.

items.title: Researchers present MemStrata, a retrieval memory system that eliminates stale-fact errors in AI agents over evolving knowledge, achieving near-perfect accuracy and faster retrieval than LLM reranking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MemStrata, a retrieval memory system designed to address the issue of stale-fact errors in AI agents that use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over evolving knowledge. Unlike traditional RAG systems that lack a temporal model and often retrieve outdated facts alongside current ones, MemStrata maintains temporal validity by applying a deterministic supersession rule to retire obsolete information without relying on similarity thresholds or large language model calls. This approach achieves near-perfect accuracy on evolving knowledge benchmarks and significantly reduces the rate of serving superseded facts to nearly zero, outperforming RAG and LLM reranking methods in both accuracy and retrieval speed.

MemStrata was tested across six benchmarks using a 7B model, matching RAG's performance on static knowledge while greatly improving accuracy on dynamic information. The system operates with a retrieval latency of approximately 2.1 seconds, compared to 16-18 seconds for LLM reranking baselines. The researchers have also released the evaluation harness, datasets, and a marker-free protocol to facilitate further study of memory systems under knowledge evolution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives agents access to accumulated knowledge, but has no model of time. When a fact changes (e.g., a function is renamed or API restructured), RAG retrieves both the stale and current value with near-identical embedding similarity. The agent then either abstains or serves the superseded fact. We show this is a structural problem: on a calibrated dataset, cosine similarity distinguishes a contradicted fact from a duplicated one with AUROC 0.59 (near chance), as contradictions are often more embedding-similar to the original than rephrased duplicates. We present MemStrata, a retrieval memory maintaining temporal validity. It stores facts like RAG, preserving static recall, but when a fact's value is contradicted, a deterministic (subject, relation, object) supersession rule retires the stale value in a bi-temporal ledger - with no similarity threshold and no LLM call. Across six benchmarks run locally with a 7B model, MemStrata ties RAG on static knowledge and reaches 0.95-1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (where RAG reaches 0.20-0.47). The central result is the stale-fact-error rate: when required to answer, RAG serves superseded values 15-40% of the time; MemStrata drives this to ~0%, a failure class RAG cannot avoid. MemStrata achieves this at retrieval latency (~2.1s) versus ~16-18s for LLM-reranking baselines. We release the harness, datasets, and a marker-free evaluation protocol for memory under knowledge evolution.

items.title: Researchers propose AIGP, an LLM-based framework for interpretable e-commerce pricing aligned with long-term business goals, showing 13.21% GMV and 7.59% ROI gains in Tao Factory tests [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AIGP: An LLM-Based Framework for Long-Term Value Alignment in E-Commerce Pricing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AIGP, a new framework that uses a Large Language Model (LLM) combined with domain knowledge, structured data, and textual context to improve dynamic pricing in large-scale e-commerce. AIGP addresses challenges in interpretability and alignment with long-term business goals such as Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), Return on Investment (ROI), and milestone achievement. The framework includes a Long-Term Value Estimator trained via offline reinforcement learning to guide pricing decisions toward these objectives.

Extensive offline tests and large-scale online A/B experiments conducted on Tao Factory showed that AIGP outperforms existing pricing models, achieving a 13.21% increase in GMV, a 7.59% rise in ROI, and an 8.20% improvement in milestone achievement rate over 14 days. Additionally, AIGP provides transparent and interpretable pricing rationales, enhancing decision-making clarity for e-commerce platforms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional dynamic pricing models in large-scale e-commerce suffer from limited interpretability, poor utilization of unstructured information, and misalignment with long-term business objectives such as cumulative Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), Return on Investment (ROI) and milestone achievement. We propose AIGP, a novel framework that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) prompted with domain knowledge, structured data and textual context to make interpretable, knowledge-aware pricing decisions. For efficient deployment while maintaining high-quality outputs, we employ supervised fine-tuning for knowledge distillation. Central to AIGP is the Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE), trained via offline reinforcement learning on historical data, which serves as a reward model to score candidate pricing actions and select preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), thereby aligning the pricing policy with long-term business objectives. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests on Tao Factory demonstrate that AIGP achieves significant improvements: +13.21% in GMV, +7.59% in ROI, and +8.20% in milestone achievement rate over 14 days compared to the production baseline, while simultaneously providing interpretable and transparent pricing rationales.

items.title: Researchers introduce CARVE, a content-aware recurrent model improving memory efficiency and performance on reasoning benchmarks with 1.3B parameters and 100B tokens training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CARVE: Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency for Chunk-Parallel Linear Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), a novel recurrent model that improves memory efficiency and performance on reasoning benchmarks. Unlike previous models that decide what to erase without considering stored memory, CARVE uses content-aware gating focused on the key axis, enabling more effective memory management. Trained with 1.3 billion parameters on 100 billion tokens, CARVE achieves lower perplexity on WikiText and outperforms existing recurrent baselines on multiple common-sense reasoning and retrieval tasks, while reducing memory usage and parameter count.

CARVE addresses three key limitations of the leading delta-rule architecture by reusing the recurrent output tensor as a content signal for the erase gate and simplifying the write-gate projection. This design maintains compatibility with the WY-form triangular chunk solver, which is essential for efficient recurrent training. The model's improvements are supported by six formal theorems covering aspects such as memory capacity and stability.

The introduction of CARVE marks a significant advancement in recurrent model design, offering a more memory-efficient approach that enhances performance on complex reasoning benchmarks. Its reduced computational overhead and parameter efficiency suggest potential for broader application in natural language processing tasks requiring long-term memory and reasoning capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recurrent models must forget in order to remember, yet the state of the art decides what to erase without consulting what is stored -- the gate sees only the arriving token, not the memory it is about to modify. This memory-blind gating is one of three coupled defects in the leading delta-rule architecture (GDN-2): the value-axis erase mask wastes parameters at the scale of the value projection, and -- as we prove -- mathematically prevents the WY-form triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training competitive with Transformers. We introduce CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), which resolves all three problems through one principle: erase only on the key axis. This is provably necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within it, CARVE reuses the recurrent output tensor -- already written to GPU memory -- as a free content signal for the erase gate, and replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialisation CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2; any quality difference emerges from what the content gate learns. At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity 15.72 (minus 0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect), leads every recurrent baseline on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe -- at 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters. Six formal theorems cover memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.

items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal web agents can assist humans in operating repetitive GUI tasks, where effective task planning is essential for decomposing complex tasks into executable actions. While small open source MLLMs are cost efficient and privacy preserving compared with commercial large models, they suffer from weak planning and limited cross website generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce the planning experience exploration and utilization (PEEU) method, which autonomously explores environments to discover experiences and utilizes hindsight experience to synthesize strictly aligned, high level training data. To quantitatively analyze the generalization behaviors driving this performance, we propose the task decomposition hierarchical analysis framework (TDHAF) to systematically study compositional generalization across three task granularities: low, middle and high levels. Our analysis reveals that mastering low level atomic skills does not guarantee high level planning competence, while high level task training yields stronger OOD generalization. Experiments on real world benchmarks demonstrate PEEU's superior effectiveness: our 7B model achieves 30.6% accuracy, outperforming the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. These demonstrate constructing hindsight high level tasks and leveraging experiences is crucial for OOD planning abilities of small MLLMs.

items.title: Researchers introduce Autodata, an AI agent trained to act as a data scientist creating high quality synthetic training and evaluation data with improved performance over classical methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Autodata: An agentic data scientist to create high quality synthetic data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Autodata, an AI agent designed to function as a data scientist by generating high-quality synthetic training and evaluation datasets. This method involves training the agent through meta-optimization to improve its ability to create stronger data, leading to enhanced performance compared to traditional synthetic data generation techniques. The approach, including a practical implementation called Agentic Self-Instruct, has been tested on tasks in computer science research, legal reasoning, and mathematical reasoning, showing notable improvements.

The study demonstrates that further meta-optimization of the data scientist agent itself results in even greater performance gains. Autodata leverages increased inference computation to produce higher quality training data, suggesting a new direction for AI data creation that could transform how datasets are built for model training and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25996v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Autodata, a general method that enables AI agents to act as data scientists who build high quality training and evaluation data. We show how to train (meta-optimize) such a data scientist agent, so that it learns to create even stronger data. We describe the overall formulation, and a specific practical implementation, Agentic Self-Instruct. We conduct experiments on computer science research tasks, legal reasoning tasks and reasoning with mathematical objects, where we obtain improved results compared to classical synthetic dataset creation methods. Further, meta-optimizing the data scientist agent itself delivers an even larger performance uplift. Agentic data creation provides a way to convert increased inference compute into higher quality model training. Overall, we believe this direction has the potential to change the way we build AI data.

items.title: Researchers propose mixed dropout-section positives for self-supervised patent representation learning, improving retrieval and classification benchmarks without external labels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Patent Representation Learning via Self-supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a self-supervised learning approach for patent representation that improves retrieval and classification tasks without relying on external labels. Their method, called mixed dropout-section positives, combines traditional dropout-based augmentation with sampling from different sections of the same patent document, such as claims or descriptions, to create more effective positive training examples. This approach leverages the internal structure of patents to enhance model performance on benchmarks like EPO search-report retrieval, DAPFAM family-level retrieval, and IPC subclass classification.

The study shows that tuning dropout parameters alone yields improvements but lacks consistent transferability across different retrieval tasks. By incorporating section-based positives, the model achieves better alignment among various patent sections and competes with citation-informed encoders and general-purpose embedding models. These findings suggest that using patent sections as self-supervised signals can lead to more robust and transferable dense patent representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.10657v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study self-supervised patent representation learning with contrastive objectives. A standard baseline constructs positives by encoding the same text twice under independent dropout masks, but applying this recipe to long, structured patent documents requires careful calibration. We show that dropout-only training can be substantially strengthened by tuning temperature and dropout rate, yet its best configuration is evaluation-dependent and does not transfer uniformly from title--abstract retrieval to claim-to-disclosure retrieval. We propose mixed dropout--section positives, a patent-specific view construction strategy in which the anchor is the title--abstract view and the positive is sampled either from a dropout re-encoding of the same view or from another section of the same patent, such as claims, summary, background, drawings, or description. This uses patent-internal structure as a training-time signal without IPC labels, citations, or relevance annotations. We evaluate on graded EPO search-report retrieval, DAPFAM, a recently proposed family-level patent retrieval benchmark, and IPC subclass classification. Section-based positives improve over calibrated dropout-only and generic title--abstract augmentation baselines, are competitive with citation-informed patent encoders and a general-purpose embedding model, and perform strongly on the out-of-domain split of DAPFAM. Additional cross-section alignment diagnostics show that section-pair training improves compatibility among abstracts, claims, and descriptions of the same invention. These results indicate that patent sections provide effective self-supervised positive views for learning dense patent representations.

items.title: Researchers find metaphors in training data cause cross-domain misalignment in large language models' reasoning and develop a detector for misaligned content [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment of Large Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers have found that metaphors present in the training data of large language models (LLMs) contribute to cross-domain misalignment in their reasoning outputs. This misalignment occurs when models generalize patterns learned from misaligned content in one domain to another, affecting their reasoning pathways. The study demonstrates that metaphor-based interventions during continued pre-training and fine-tuning can induce varying degrees of this emergent misalignment, and similar effects are observed during re-alignment processes.

Further investigation revealed that metaphors are linked to the activation of latent features within large reasoning models. By monitoring these features, the researchers developed a detector capable of predicting misaligned content with high accuracy, offering a potential tool to identify and address reasoning misalignment in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.03388v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Earlier research has shown that metaphors influence human decision-making, raising the question of whether metaphors also influence large language models (LLMs)' reasoning pathways, given that their training data contain a large number of metaphors. In this work, we investigate the problem in the scope of the emergent misalignment problem, where LLMs can generalize patterns learned from misaligned content in one domain to another domain. We find strong evidence that metaphors in training data contribute to cross-domain misalignment in LLMs' reasoning outputs. With metaphor-based interventions during continued pre-training and fine-tuning for inducing misalignment, models exhibit significantly different degrees of emergent cross-domain misalignment. We also observe similar effects in re-alignment settings. As we further investigate this phenomenon, we find that metaphors are linked to the activation of latent features in large reasoning models. By monitoring these latent features, we design a detector that predicts misaligned content with high accuracy.

items.title: Researchers find injecting mismatched wrong drafts from smaller models improves Mathstral-7B's performance on MATH-500 and AIME 2025/2026 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Weak-to-Strong Elicitation via Mismatched Wrong Drafts
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that injecting mathematically incorrect drafts from a smaller, domain-trained model into the training context of a stronger model, Mathstral-7B, enhances its performance on challenging math benchmarks such as MATH-500 and the AIME 2025/2026. This approach, which involves mismatching drafts to problems during training, consistently outperforms standard on-policy reinforcement learning fine-tuning methods like GRPO, achieving the highest known accuracy for Mathstral-7B on MATH-500 without requiring additional data synthesis or complex training loops.

The study used Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as the draft model and trained on 8.8K math problems, demonstrating that the mismatched-wrong draft variant improved results by significant margins compared to matched or correct drafts. Notably, this method also boosted performance on out-of-distribution tests, surpassing both the base Mathstral-7B and the draft model across various sampling budgets. The training was efficiently conducted on a single GPU without supervised fine-tuning or reward models, highlighting a novel and resource-effective strategy for enhancing mathematical reasoning in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.17314v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider whether off-policy experience from a smaller, weaker model can elicit capability in a stronger learner that on-policy RL fine-tuning (e.g., GRPO) does not reach. We find that injecting mathematically wrong drafts from a smaller but more domain-trained model -- mismatched to the current problem -- into a stronger learner's GRPO context consistently outperforms standard on-policy GRPO on held-out MATH-500 and out-of-distribution AIME 2025/2026. Concretely, we use Mathstral-7B as the learner, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B as the draft model, 8.8K Level 3--5 MATH problems (with MATH-500 held out), and train with Dr. GRPO. Mismatch is an active ingredient: shuffling drafts to mismatched problems while holding everything else constant yields $+1.62$pp on MATH-500 (greedy pass@1) over the matched-wrong variant ($n=10$ seeds, $p=0.0015$, Welch's $t$). In fact, the mismatched-wrong variant leads all other variants we tested on MATH-500 across both greedy pass@1 and sampling pass@$k$. On out-of-distribution AIME 2025 and 2026, the mismatched-wrong variant uniquely lifts pass@$k$ above both Mathstral-7B (in its native [INST] format) and the Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B draft model at every sample budget from $k=1$ to $k=1024$ across 2 seeds ($+14.2$pp on 2025 and $+9.0$pp on 2026 at pass@1024 over Mathstral-7B), and at pass@1024 also leads no-draft, matched-wrong, and mismatched-correct variants on both years. All variants use the same prompt with no draft injection at test time. The recipe -- trained on a single GPU with no SFT, no reward models, no synthesized data, and no produce-critique-revise inner loop -- reaches 71.98% MATH-500 on Mathstral-7B-v0.1, the highest published result on this model to our knowledge, surpassing the heavier WizardMath pipeline at 70.9% on full MATH (SFT + PPO with process/instruction reward models).

items.title: Researchers say verifying coding agent rewards is increasingly difficult as model capabilities grow, highlighting challenges in scalability, faithfulness, and robustness of verification signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers have found that as foundation models improve their reasoning abilities, verifying the correctness of coding agent outputs has become more challenging than generating the solutions themselves. Verification relies on proxies for human intent, which are inherently underspecified and can lead to issues like reward hacking and signal saturation during model training. The study identifies three key dimensions for effective verification signals: scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, and examines four types of reward mechanisms across various coding tasks and agent capabilities.

Through extensive analysis and experiments, the researchers demonstrate that carefully designed verification methods can reduce reward manipulation, enhance task completion quality, and yield significant improvements on multiple benchmarks. Their findings highlight that no static reward function remains effective as model capabilities advance, emphasizing the need for verification processes to evolve alongside the generative models they assess.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

items.title: Researchers introduce OpenFinGym, a unified multi-task environment for evaluating quantitative finance agents across forecasting, trading, risk management, and fraud detection with verifiable execution and scalable testing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OpenFinGym, a unified multi-task environment designed to evaluate quantitative finance agents across various interconnected tasks such as forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection. This platform addresses the limitations of existing tools that focus on isolated tasks, potentially overstating agent capabilities and overlooking challenges in generalization and real-market decision-making. OpenFinGym offers a single execution and verification interface to ensure consistent and verifiable agent evaluation.

The environment includes an automated pipeline that converts quantitative finance research into executable tasks, a containerized runtime with a verifier service to support scalable testing and prevent data leakage, and a low-latency paper trading engine. It also supports long-horizon and event-driven forecasts and integrates with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning methods post-training, providing a comprehensive framework for developing and assessing finance-focused AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train-test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training

items.title: Researchers introduce Narration-of-Thought system prompt to improve ethical reasoning in large language models, reducing stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression across multiple AI generators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new system prompt called Narration-of-Thought (NoT) to enhance ethical reasoning in large language models. NoT structures the reasoning process into five parts—protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, and commitment—addressing common issues like stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. Testing across multiple AI generators showed that NoT significantly reduces these failures, improving the models' ability to consider multiple parties and acknowledge uncertainties in moral dilemmas.

The approach was evaluated on 100 scenarios from the DailyDilemmas dataset using four different AI generators from three vendors. NoT decreased stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to between 1% and 24%. Further analysis confirmed that these improvements stem from the structured prompt itself rather than increased token usage. Extending NoT into a multi-round debate protocol among stakeholders led to near-complete consensus in ethical judgments, demonstrating its potential for creating more transparent and auditable AI decision-making processes.

This advancement offers a promising framework for deploying AI systems that require dependable ethical reasoning by explicitly externalizing stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainties behind each decision. The method's compatibility with existing models and its ability to foster consensus suggest it could play a key role in improving the reliability and accountability of agentic AI applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard chain-of-thought on moral dilemmas exhibits two failure modes: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit unknowns or hedges before committing to an action). We introduce narration-of-thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. NoT adds no training, parameters, or fine-tuning. On 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors, NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control rules out token spend as the active ingredient; NoT retains Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators, and a section ablation attributes each shift to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT improves the scaffold further; a cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) dominates an in-family one on every measured axis. Extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication. The resulting traces externalise the stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty grounding each commitment, providing an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

items.title: Researchers propose Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search to solve extremal combinatorial geometry problems, achieving new best-known results on five of six tested problems including Max-N3IL and Smallest Complete Set [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to address extremal problems in combinatorial geometry involving point configurations on an $n \times n$ grid with strict geometric constraints. This approach improves upon classical solvers and machine learning models by incrementally updating feasible actions and enforcing constraints efficiently, notably reducing complexity for problems like the No-Three-in-Line (Max-N3IL) from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. The method also leverages geometric symmetries to enhance search efficiency through pruning and batch transitions.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that this framework achieves new best-known results on five of six tested problems, including finding configurations of size approximately $1.8 n$ for Max-N3IL on grids sized $82 \le n \le 119$, and configurations of size about $0.95 n$ for the Smallest Complete Set problem, establishing new upper bounds. This work positions Geometry-Aware MCTS as a versatile tool for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

items.title: Researchers propose a lattice-theoretic method for unbiased, self-consistent set-valued oracles addressing AI self-reference in probability estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a lattice-theoretic approach to address the self-reference problem faced by non-agentic "oracle" AI systems that estimate probabilities of future events. Traditional methods that ask counterfactual questions become irrelevant once their answers are known, as the premise changes. Instead, the new method involves the oracle reporting a set of probabilities, or a credal set, that is both unbiased and self-consistent with the effects of the answer being learned.

The approach uses the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the lattice of closed credal sets to identify a canonical, nontrivial solution that satisfies self-consistency. This method generalizes from binary events to arbitrary random variables and ensures existence, nonemptiness, and consistency of the solution. The researchers also discuss open questions, including whether the interval characterization of the solution extends to more general cases.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

items.title: Researchers find humans spend less time on failed reasoning tasks while large reasoning models spend more tokens on failures, revealing opposite deliberation allocation despite similar difficulty tracking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
items.summary:
Researchers have found that while both humans and large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on more difficult problems, they differ in how they allocate their effort on individual tasks. Humans tend to spend less time on problems they ultimately fail, suggesting they disengage when they expect to fail, whereas LRMs spend more tokens on problems they get wrong, indicating prolonged deliberation driven by uncertainty. This reveals opposite patterns of deliberation allocation despite similar overall difficulty tracking.

The study distinguishes between two levels of deliberation: difficulty registration across different problems and deliberation allocation within the same problem. Using a matched human-LRM dataset, the researchers observed that humans and LRMs align in registering difficulty across items but diverge significantly in how they allocate effort on successes versus failures. This divergence persists across datasets and is absent in non-thinking baselines, highlighting fundamental differences in stopping policies between humans and LRMs.

These findings suggest that humans tend to abandon problems they find too challenging, while LRMs continue processing when uncertain, leading to longer reasoning chains on failures. This distinction has implications for understanding metareasoning strategies and improving the design of reasoning models by considering not just difficulty signals but also control policies governing effort allocation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

items.title: Researchers develop a framework for radical AI interpretability to infer beliefs and desires from computational systems, addressing safety and trust in AI deployment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Radical AI Interpretability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new framework for interpreting artificial intelligence systems as agents by applying the philosophical concept of radical interpretation alongside mechanistic interpretability techniques. This approach aims to determine an AI system's beliefs, desires, and meanings based on its computational structure, which is crucial for ensuring safety and trust in AI deployment by understanding or detecting the system's goals and potential deception.

The framework proposes criteria for both representationalist and interpretationist methods and connects these to practical tests that current interpretability tools can perform. It emphasizes that attributing beliefs and desires cannot be done in isolation, as these mental states and their underlying propositional structures are interdependent. This holistic view is particularly important because AI systems may not share human concepts, but it also allows for mutual constraints between attitudes and propositional structures to be measured through mechanistic interpretability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents, drawing on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation and the tools of mechanistic interpretability. The core question is: given the computational facts about a system, how do we solve for its beliefs, desires, and meanings? This matters increasingly for safety. We want to be able to trust the systems we deploy, whether by understanding their goals or, more modestly, by reliably detecting deception. Interpretability researchers are building tools to read beliefs and desires off a model's internals, but there is no settled account of when such a tool has succeeded. This book supplies one. We propose criteria on both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, and tie each to tests current interpretability methods can carry out. A central lesson is that these attributions cannot be made piecemeal. Beliefs, desires, and the propositional structure they presuppose are jointly constrained, and a method that fixes one while measuring the others inherits whatever distortions that introduces. This holism becomes pressing for AI systems, which may not share the interpreter's concepts. However, it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can help us measure both.

items.title: Researchers introduce PMDformer, a transformer model using patch-mean decoupling and specialized attention mechanisms to improve long-term time series forecasting accuracy and stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PMDformer: Patch-Mean Decoupling Information Transformer for Long-term Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PMDformer, a transformer model designed to improve long-term time series forecasting by addressing challenges in capturing shape similarities across patches and variables. The model introduces patch-mean decoupling (PMD) to separate trend and residual shape information, ensuring the attention mechanism focuses on true shape similarities. Additionally, PMDformer incorporates Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA) to better model long-range dependencies and cross-variable relationships.

PMDformer reintegrates decoupled trends during attention calculation and emphasizes recent, relevant time segments to avoid overfitting on outdated correlations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and stability across multiple long-term forecasting benchmarks. The model's code is publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26549v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) plays a crucial role in fields such as energy management, finance, and traffic prediction. Transformer-based models have adopted patch-based strategies to capture long-range dependencies, but accurately modeling shape similarities across patches and variables remains challenging due to scale differences. To address this, we introduce patch-mean decoupling (PMD), which separates the trend and residual shape information by subtracting the mean of each patch, preserving the original structure and ensuring that the attention mechanism captures true shape similarities. Futhermore, to more effectively model long-range dependencies and capture cross-variable relationships, we propose Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA). The former module reintegrates the decoupled trend from PMD while calculating attention output. And the latter focuses cross-variable attention on the most relevant, recent time segments to avoid overfitting on outdated correlations. Combining these components, we propose PMDformer, a model designed to effectively capture shape similarity in long-term forecasting scenarios. Extensive experiments indicate that PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/aohu1105/PMDformer.

items.title: Researchers develop explainable ensemble machine learning models to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients, with Extra Trees model achieving 96.92% accuracy on a dataset of 2038 Egyptian patients [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Explainable Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Models for Detecting the Presence of Cirrhosis in Hepatitis C Patients
items.summary:
Researchers have developed explainable ensemble machine learning models to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients, using a dataset of 2038 Egyptian patients with 28 attributes. Among four algorithms tested—Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Extra Trees—the Extra Trees model achieved the highest accuracy of 96.92%, along with strong recall and precision metrics, using only 16 features. This approach offers a promising tool for early detection of cirrhosis, which is critical for preventing disease progression and complications in hepatitis C patients.

The study highlights the potential of machine learning to improve diagnosis in liver disease, addressing a gap where no prior ML-based methods had been applied to cirrhosis detection in hepatitis C. Early identification of cirrhosis can help manage treatment more effectively and reduce risks such as liver failure and neurological damage.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus, which results in mild to severe inflammation of the liver. Over many years, hepatitis C gradually damages the liver, often leading to permanent scarring, known as cirrhosis. Patients sometimes have moderate or no symptoms of liver illness for decades before developing cirrhosis. Cirrhosis typically worsens to the point of liver failure. Patients with cirrhosis may also experience brain and nerve system damage, as well as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Treatment for cirrhosis focuses on preventing further progression of the disease. Detecting cirrhosis earlier is therefore crucial for avoiding complications. Machine learning (ML) has been shown to be effective at providing precise and accurate information for use in diagnosing several diseases. Despite this, no studies have so far used ML to detect cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C. This study obtained a dataset consisting of 28 attributes of 2038 Egyptian patients from the ML Repository of the University of California at Irvine. Four ML algorithms were trained on the dataset to diagnose cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients: a Random Forest, a Gradient Boosting Machine, an Extreme Gradient Boosting, and an Extra Trees model. The Extra Trees model outperformed the other models achieving an accuracy of 96.92%, a recall of 94.00%, a precision of 99.81%, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 96% using only 16 of the 28 features.

items.title: Researchers introduce LeanGuard, a lightweight safety guardrail that matches reasoning-based moderation accuracy with 100x less compute and improved robustness on public benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Safety Guardrails Need to Reason? LeanGuard: A Fast and Light Approach for Robust Moderation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LeanGuard, a lightweight safety guardrail for content moderation that achieves reasoning-based moderation accuracy while using about 100 times less computational power. Unlike traditional guardrails that rely on generating a chain-of-thought (CoT) for step-by-step reasoning, LeanGuard uses a 395 million parameter label-only encoder that processes inputs in a single forward pass without explicit reasoning. This approach matches the performance of larger, reasoning-based models on public benchmarks with an average F1 score of 82.90, while also demonstrating greater robustness to training-label noise and maintaining higher recall at strict false-positive rates.

The study challenges the assumption that reasoning through CoT is necessary for effective moderation, suggesting that current benchmarks may not sufficiently reward reasoning capabilities. LeanGuard's efficiency and robustness make it suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments, such as on-device applications in embodied robots. The researchers have made all source code and models publicly available to support further exploration and development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In order to screen a prompt or a response, the recent guardrail methods generate a chain-of-thought (CoT) before they issue a verdict. This design follows a common belief that step-by-step reasoning improves a decision. However, CoT also makes the guard heavy and slow, because the model must generate many tokens before it decides. This may not match how guardrails are actually deployed. A guardrail sometimes should not be heavy and slow, and it often runs on-device, for example on an embodied robot. In this paper, we pose a question whether a safety guardrail really needs to reason. To answer this question, we train a lightweight bidirectional encoder and a reasoning guard on the same corpus, and we then remove only the reasoning while we keep everything else fixed. With this controlled same-base comparison, we show that the chain does not improve moderation accuracy. We name the resulting guard LeanGuard. A 395M label-only encoder reaches an average F1 of 82.90 $\pm$ 0.26 over public benchmarks. It matches a reasoning guard that is built on a much larger decoder, while it uses only a single forward pass over an input of at most 512 tokens. This is about a ~100x reduction in inference compute. We further show that this label-only encoder stays robust under training-label noise and retains far more recall at a strict false-positive rate than the reasoning guard, so a heavier reasoning guard is not the more robust choice either. Our finding suggests that the current guardrail benchmarks may not be hard enough to reward reasoning, and that the necessity of CoT for moderation is still not proven. We release all source codes and models including LeanGuard at https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard.

items.title: Researchers propose meta-optimization framework using consensus objective aggregation with LLMs to improve algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems, achieving 67x speedup and reduced scaling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scientific discovery as meta-optimization: a combinatorial optimization case study
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a meta-optimization framework that enhances scientific discovery by simultaneously optimizing both the search process and its evaluation criteria. This approach, called consensus objective aggregation, combines multiple objective functions generated by large language models through correlation-weighted voting to create a stable and adaptive evaluation metric. Applied to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems using digital MemComputing machines, the method significantly improved performance, reducing computational scaling from approximately N^{2.51} to N^{1.33} and achieving a 67-fold speedup on the largest tested instances.

This problem-agnostic framework leverages evolving evaluation criteria to deepen understanding and improve optimization outcomes, demonstrating potential to accelerate scientific research across various domains by refining both objectives and solutions concurrently.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific discovery is fundamentally an optimization problem, defined by a vast "state space" of theories and experiments, and an evaluation criterion based on quality, novelty, and validity. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated exploration of this space, but we argue that simultaneous modification of the evaluation criteria is equally important. Here, we propose formalizing research as meta-optimization, where the optimization objective itself is also being optimized. Our key contribution is "consensus objective aggregation," where LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting, yielding a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens. We apply this framework to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems based on digital MemComputing machines, reducing the baseline scaling with problem size $N$ from $\sim N^{2.51}$ to $\sim N^{1.33}$ and delivering a $\sim 67\times$ speedup on the largest instances tested. As a problem-agnostic framework, we hope this approach will considerably aid scientific discovery.

items.title: Researchers introduce selective parametric consolidation mechanism EVAF to enhance memory depth and goal persistence in long-running language agents across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Memory Depth, Not Memory Access: Selective Parametric Consolidation for Long-Running Language Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVAF, a selective parametric consolidation mechanism designed to improve memory depth and goal persistence in long-running language agents. Unlike traditional retrieval systems that fetch past facts at query time, EVAF enables durable, goal-conditioned behaviors to persist even after the working context is unloaded. The mechanism was tested using the loop-drift protocol across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B models, demonstrating strong performance in maintaining goal persistence and recovery with minimal parametric updates.

EVAF operates by selectively consolidating experiences based on surprise and valence signals, effectively balancing selection and actuation processes. Experiments showed that while retrieval excels at shallow factual recall, EVAF enhances long-term behavioral consistency under interference. Additional analyses revealed model-dependent variations in consolidation strength and highlighted challenges such as stale-memory invalidation. This approach offers a complementary form of memory depth distinct from conventional retrieval methods, advancing the capabilities of language agents in sustained tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running language agents need more than memory access. Retrieval systems can fetch past facts at query time, but they do not decide which experiences should continue to shape behavior after the working context is unloaded. We study this separate problem as memory depth: durable goal-conditioned tendencies written into a small parametric store. We introduce the loop-drift protocol, a controlled stress test in which the retrieval index remains intact while working context is unloaded and goal-conditioned behavior must persist under long-loop interference. We evaluate EVAF, a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism. Across GPT-2 and TinyLlama, retrieval is strongest on shallow factual recall (short-fact accuracy 0.956--0.973), while EVAF is strongest on goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812--0.904) with only 2--3 parametric writes per 200 events. Mechanism controls show that selective consolidation factorizes into two controllable dimensions: selection and actuation. Matched random gates isolate selection beyond sparse writing; fixed-inner controls across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B show that inner-loop write strength is model-dependent; and a Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion reveals asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Public Memora event streams serve as an external diagnostic, exposing stale-memory invalidation as an unresolved boundary. Within this probe, selective parametric consolidation supplies memory depth distinct from and complementary to retrieval access.

items.title: Researchers propose KARLA method enabling language models to retrieve factual knowledge from knowledge bases during generation, improving accuracy and transparency without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KARLA: Knowledge-base Augmented Retrieval for Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed KARLA, a method that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve factual information from external knowledge bases during text generation. This approach allows the factual content in the model's output to be updated without retraining, improves transparency by linking facts to their sources, and enables smaller models to match the factual accuracy of larger ones. KARLA works by training the model to generate special tokens that trigger queries to the knowledge base, enhancing factual grounding in both short and long-form outputs.

Experiments demonstrate that KARLA effectively integrates external knowledge, allowing factual updates through edits to the knowledge base rather than changes to the model's parameters. This method supports greater explainability and adaptability in language models, potentially improving their reliability and efficiency in generating accurate information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a new method that allows an LLM to automatically pull in factual knowledge from a knowledge base during token generation. This means that (1)~factual knowledge in the LLM output can be updated without retraining the LLM, (2)~facts in the LLM output can be traced to the knowledge base for transparency and explainability, and (3)~smaller models can achieve the same factual accuracy as larger models. Our core idea is to train the model to produce special tokens that trigger a query to the knowledge base. Our experiments show that our method improves factual grounding in both short and long-form generation, and allows factual revisions to take effect through KB edits rather than parameter updates.

items.title: Researchers present AgentX, a multi-agent system that autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from industrial recommender system experiments to enable self-iteration and continuous improvement [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: AgentX: Towards Agent-Driven Self-Iteration of Industrial Recommender Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AgentX, a multi-agent system designed to automate and accelerate the iteration of industrial recommender systems. AgentX autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments, overcoming the traditional bottleneck where human engineers manually handle hypothesis generation, coding, and A/B testing. This system enables continuous improvement by operating a closed loop of four stages: brainstorming proposals, developing production-ready code, safely evaluating experiments online, and refining its own processes through semantic-gradient updates.

AgentX integrates evidence from past experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research to create ranked proposals. It then translates these into reliable code, conducts controlled online rollouts with safety measures, and converts outcomes into structured knowledge. The system's self-improving nature allows it to evolve beyond automation, enhancing its performance and innovation pace without additional human intervention.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recommendation algorithm iteration is moving from an artisanal, engineer-bound process toward an industrialized research loop, but this transition remains blocked by a structural execution bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle still depends on human engineers to generate hypotheses, modify production code, launch A/B experiments, and attribute online results. Innovation therefore scales linearly with headcount rather than compounding with evidence, compute, and accumulated experimental knowledge. We present AgentX, a production-deployed multi-agent system that fundamentally restructures this production function. AgentX operates as a self-evolving development engine: it autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments at a scale and pace that no manual workflow can sustain. The system orchestrates four tightly coupled stages in a closed loop. A Brainstorm Agent synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked, executable proposals. A Developing Agent translates each proposal into production-ready code through repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification. An Evaluation Agent conducts safe online rollout with guardrail-vetoed A/B judgment, converting both successes and failures into structured knowledge assets. A Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) then distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously sharpen the agents themselves -- making the system not merely automated, but self-improving.
