items.title: Researchers propose Einstein World Models to enhance LLM reasoning with visual-temporal rollouts as inspectable hypotheses for complex thought experiments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Einstein World Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Einstein World Models (EWMs), a new framework designed to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by integrating visual-temporal rollouts as part of their reasoning process. EWMs enable LLMs to generate and inspect short visual simulations of scenarios, treating these visualizations as hypotheses to support complex thought beyond what text alone can achieve. This approach extends the traditional tool-calling abilities of LLMs, such as web search or code execution, into the realm of visual thought experiments.

In this model, the LLM interacts with a specialized world-module to produce these visual rollouts, which are not definitive answers but serve as inspectable elements that aid further reasoning. The proposal addresses the challenge of whether visualizing counterfactual events can complement language to improve complex reasoning, suggesting that such multimodal integration could advance the intelligence and problem-solving skills of AI systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

items.title: Researchers propose semantic early-stopping for iterative LLM agent loops to reduce token use by 38% without quality loss, validated on multi-hop question answering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a semantic early-stopping method for iterative loops in multi-agent large language models (LLMs), such as a Writer-Critic setup, to reduce unnecessary token usage without compromising answer quality. Unlike traditional fixed iteration caps that stop processing after a set number of rounds regardless of improvement, this approach halts the loop when consecutive draft embeddings show minimal semantic change and the answer's quality plateaus. This method was validated on multi-hop question answering tasks, achieving a 38% reduction in token use while maintaining comparable performance.

The study provides a theoretical foundation proving deterministic termination and well-definedness of the stopping criterion, supported by machine-checked proofs. It also introduces an efficient evaluation protocol that replays stopping policies over identical draft trajectories to fairly compare efficiency and quality. Empirical results on the HotpotQA dataset demonstrate that a judge-free semantic stopper effectively balances token savings and answer quality, whereas a quality-gated variant incurs higher costs due to frequent judging. The findings suggest that future work should focus on identifying the best iteration round rather than merely deciding when to stop.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

items.title: Researchers propose BINEVAL, a binary-question framework for interpretable and task-agnostic LLM evaluation that improves prompt optimization and outperforms baselines on factual consistency benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced BINEVAL, a novel framework for evaluating large language model (LLM) outputs by breaking down evaluation criteria into simple binary questions. This approach generates detailed, interpretable feedback and overall scores that are easier to analyze and use for improving prompts. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

items.title: Researchers identify a co-failure ceiling limiting accuracy gains from combining 67 large language models across routing, voting, and mixture-of-agents methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a fundamental limit, termed the co-failure ceiling, that restricts accuracy improvements when combining multiple large language models (LLMs) through methods like routing, voting, and mixture-of-agents. This limit is defined by the rate at which all models simultaneously fail on the same query, a metric called beta, which traditional diagnostics like average pairwise error correlation cannot capture. The study analyzed 67 models from 21 providers and found that the observed co-failure rates are higher than predicted by standard models, indicating a significant underestimation of joint errors in multi-model systems.

The research highlights that gains from combining models primarily arise when models fail on different questions rather than simply adding more models. Experiments showed that on tasks such as open-ended mathematics and execution-graded code, the co-failure rate remains substantial, limiting the maximum achievable accuracy. Additionally, changing answer formats from multiple-choice to free-response increased the co-failure rate, suggesting that failure patterns depend more on answer format than subject matter.

These findings imply that without strong query-level routing signals, combining multiple models rarely outperforms the single best model on verifiable tasks. The study provides a statistical bound on the maximum accuracy gain achievable by ensemble methods, offering a practical benchmark for future multi-model system designs and emphasizing the importance of diverse failure modes over sheer model quantity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router. Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

items.title: Researchers present Know2Guess, a contamination-aware multi-zone benchmark with 1,200 items for evaluating knowledge boundaries and abstention behavior in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Know2Guess: A Contamination-Aware Multi-Zone Benchmark for Knowledge-Boundary Evaluation in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Know2Guess, a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark designed to evaluate large language models' ability to distinguish between supported answers and unsupported guesses while accounting for data contamination and prompt variability. The benchmark includes 1,200 items across five domains with explicit abstention expectations and contamination-risk metadata, enabling assessment of models' transitions from answering to abstaining when knowledge is uncertain. Evaluations of models such as FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct reveal that while some instruction-tuned models show selective transitions to abstention, challenges remain in calibration and refusal behavior, with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct demonstrating the highest overall reliability.

The benchmark employs dual parsing methods and various prompt configurations to ensure robustness and reproducibility in auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting factors affecting model reliability. This dataset and evaluation protocol provide a valuable resource for advancing the assessment of large language models' knowledge boundaries and decision-making processes. The Know2Guess dataset is publicly accessible for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable evaluation of large language models should separate supported answering from unsupported guessing without conflating either with data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, or generic refusal behavior. We present a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark for measuring the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under frozen build-time labels. The benchmark contains 1,200 items across five domains, explicit abstention expectations, contamination-risk metadata, and dual parsing with an official strict parser plus a normalized robustness parser. We evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct models under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. The benchmark is not solved by generic non-answer behavior: FLAN baselines remain weak on productive abstention, while stronger instruction-tuned models expose a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration remains poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions. The benchmark therefore provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability.The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/renweimeng/Know2Guess-A-Contamination-Aware-Multi-Zone-Benchmark.

items.title: Researchers find post-training on helpfulness data degrades mid-trained compassion values in Llama 3.1 8B model, while coding-domain post-training better preserves these values across languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Helpfulness Hurts: Domain-Dependent Degradation of Mid-Trained Compassion Values Under Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers examined how different post-training domains affect the retention of compassion values in the Llama 3.1 8B language model, which was mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data. They compared supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using helpfulness-focused datasets versus coding-focused datasets, evaluating the model's performance on benchmarks related to animal harm and moral reasoning. The study found that post-training on helpfulness data significantly degraded the model's compassion values and moral reasoning in English, while coding-domain post-training better preserved these values across multiple languages.

The degradation effect was consistent across two independent helpfulness datasets and training methods, with a notable drop in compassion and moral reasoning scores. However, the decline in moral reasoning did not appear in multilingual evaluations, suggesting that compassion values instilled during mid-training are more deeply encoded and transfer better across languages than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These findings indicate that coding-domain post-training may be a preferable approach for maintaining value-laden traits in language models without compromising their general reasoning abilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard post-training pipelines apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to make language models helpful, but these processes may inadvertently degrade values instilled during pre-training. We investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a Llama 3.1 8B model mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, using both SFT (helpfulness via Dolly-15k vs. coding via Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness via RLHFlow vs. coding via Magicoder), evaluated on the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty). Helpfulness training significantly degrades animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two independent helpfulness datasets and two training paradigms. On English MORU items, helpfulness training degrades general moral reasoning by 25.5 percentage points (46.4% vs. 71.9%), a striking gap that rivals the compassion effect in magnitude. However, this effect does not transfer cross-lingually: on the multilingual MORU benchmark, the domain effect disappears (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). In contrast, the animal compassion effect transfers consistently across languages, with Magicoder's AHB percentage-point gain over the base model 4.5 times larger on non-English items than English items. This divergence suggests that values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These results suggest that, for labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training without harming general reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Study finds large language models perform well on text-only statics problems but struggle with diagrams and multi-step reasoning in mechanical engineering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Investigating LLM's Problem Solving Capability -- a Study on Statics Questions
items.summary:
A recent study evaluated the problem-solving abilities of large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT, on mechanical engineering statics problems. The research found that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics questions, their accuracy declines when diagrams are included and when problems require multi-step reasoning. This suggests that the models face challenges in integrating visual information consistently throughout complex solution processes.

The study used a model distillation approach to extract 25 text-only statics questions and created additional datasets by adding diagrams and altering numerical values. Analysis indicated that the reduced performance was not mainly due to image recognition issues but rather difficulties in multi-step reasoning and applying visual data across successive steps. These findings highlight limitations of current LLMs in handling diagram-based and multi-step engineering problems, pointing to areas for future improvement in educational applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly influenced many aspects of society, particularly education, due to their demonstrated ability to complete assignments and examinations across a wide range of subjects. Although prior studies have examined the educational impact of LLMs, much of the existing work relies on public or open problem datasets and lacks topic-specific analysis. In engineering education, especially within mechanical engineering, systematic investigations of LLM performance on specific problem types remain limited. Instead of using traditional methods that directly ask textbook questions to an LLM tool, our study adopts a model distillation process to evaluate LLM capabilities in solving statics problems. By distilling ChatGPT, we extracted 25 text-only statics questions and further constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying their numerical values. Experimental results show that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy decreases when diagrams are introduced and the problems require multi-step reasoning. Further analysis suggests that this performance drop is not primarily caused by limitations in image recognition, but rather by difficulties in multi-step reasoning and in consistently applying extracted visual information across successive solution stages.

items.title: Researchers find assertive and explicit linguistic features in fine-tuning data increase Llama-3.2-1B's pro-animal-welfare reasoning while hedged and sensory descriptions dilute it [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Assert, don't describe: Linguistic features that shift LLM reasoning about animal welfare
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed how different linguistic features in fine-tuning data affect Llama-3.2-1B's reasoning about animal welfare. They found that assertive and explicit language, including moral vocabulary, emotion words, and narrative elements, significantly increased the model's pro-animal-welfare stance, while hedged language and sensory descriptions weakened it. First-person perspective showed no significant impact.

The study used vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a dedicated animal-welfare benchmark to measure these effects. The findings suggest that texts explicitly asserting a position are more effective in shaping language models toward pro-animal-welfare reasoning than neutral or descriptive content.

This research offers practical guidance for authors of animal-welfare content that may be used in training large language models, emphasizing the importance of clear, assertive expression to influence model behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Animal-welfare advocates produce a lot of writing, and increasingly that writing trains the language models that millions of people then ask about animal welfare. Using vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark, we measure how each of ten linguistic features changes Llama-3.2-1B's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning when used as fine-tuning data. Eight of the ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven move the model toward stronger pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two move it the other way: hedged language and concrete sensory description both dilute the pro-animal-welfare stance. First-person perspective has no statistically significant effect. The practical recommendation for anyone writing animal-welfare text that may end up in LLM training corpora: assert a position rather than describe a scene neutrally. The features that shift the model are the ones that make the writer's position explicit; the features that dilute it hold animal-welfare content but withhold stance.

items.title: Researchers show Nonviolent Communication constraints reduce conversational escalation in large language model dialogues across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reducing Conversational Escalation in Large Language Model Dialogue with Nonviolent Communication Constraints
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that applying Nonviolent Communication (NVC) principles as prompt-level constraints can reduce conversational escalation in large language model (LLM) dialogues. By reformulating NVC guidelines to discourage blame, focus on users' emotions, and promote clarification before advice, the study shows that these constraints help LLMs engage in more de-escalating behavior, especially in emotionally charged interactions involving conflict or resistance.

Using a dual-agent simulation framework across various instruction-tuned models and levels of user resistance, the research found that NVC-constrained prompting consistently stabilizes conversations and reduces escalation. These findings suggest that simple communication constraints can enhance the trustworthiness and safety of LLM dialogue systems in conflict-prone settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, frustration, and distress. While prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms such as toxic or policy-violating content, less attention has been paid to conversational behaviors that may unintentionally escalate conflict. In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can be guided toward more de-escalating dialogue behavior through lightweight prompt-level constraints derived from Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented guidelines that discourage blame attribution, emphasize attention to users' emotional experiences, and encourage clarification before advice. Using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels, we show that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users. These results suggest that simple communication constraints can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings.

items.title: Researchers present NEST-V1, a multimodal framework translating Nepali spoken words into emotion-conditioned sign language avatars with 81.1% speech recognition and 79.21% emotion accuracy for low-resource settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Low Resource Multimodal Translation of Nepali Spoken Words into Emotion-Conditioned Sign Language Avatars
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NEST-V1, a multimodal framework that translates Nepali spoken words into emotion-conditioned sign language avatars, achieving 81.1% accuracy in speech recognition and 79.21% in emotion classification. This pilot study focuses on four common Nepali words expressed in three emotional states—happy, neutral, and sad—demonstrating the system's ability to generate emotionally expressive sign language from audio input in a low-resource language setting.

The framework uses a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous automatic speech recognition and emotion detection, resulting in a lightweight model with 22.1 million parameters, suitable for edge deployment. It shows 37% greater parameter efficiency compared to separate models, based on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. This work lays the foundation for scalable, real-time, emotion-aware sign language translation systems that could enhance communication for the hearing-impaired community in low-resource environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sign language communication systems, that integrate emotional expression remain underexplored, particularly for low-resource languages. This pilot study presents NEST-V1 (Nepali Emotion and Speech Transformer - Version 1), a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that demonstrates the feasibility of generating emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on four common Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to validate our core technical approach. Our lightweight architecture employs a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. The system demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures while maintaining a lightweight footprint with only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment. This pilot work establishes the technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings and provides a scalable framework for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions. Our preliminary results indicate the viability of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems for the hearing-impaired community, with clear pathways for enhancement in subsequent development phases.

items.title: Researchers present a pipeline converting Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million instruction-response pairs to fine-tune a 12B-parameter model for specialized conversational AI in low-resource languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Lexicon to AI: A Structured-Data Pipeline for Specialized Conversational Systems in Low-Resource Languages
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a pipeline that transforms Hindi WordNet, a structured lexical database, into 1.25 million instruction-response pairs to fine-tune a 12-billion-parameter language model. This approach uses resource-efficient techniques like LoRA and 4-bit quantization to create a specialized conversational AI system tailored for low-resource languages. Evaluation with a Hindi language learning chatbot showed that this structured-knowledge-based system outperforms general-purpose models in pedagogical effectiveness while maintaining strong semantic accuracy and consistency.

The methodology demonstrates a practical alternative to traditional corpus-intensive AI training by leveraging expert-curated linguistic resources. This proof-of-concept using Hindi suggests that similar specialized AI systems can be developed for hundreds of other languages that have WordNet resources, addressing a significant gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages and enabling more effective conversational AI applications in these contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-resource languages face a critical challenge in AI development: creating specialized conversational systems without access to massive training corpora. We present a systematic methodology for transforming structured linguistic resources into specialized AI systems, demonstrating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for conversational AI development. Our approach converts Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs, fine-tunes a 12B-parameter language model using resource-efficient LoRA with 4-bit quantization. This work addresses the critical gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages, offering a practical alternative to corpus-intensive approaches and potentially enabling specialized AI development for the hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources.

items.title: Researchers develop an open-source economic index measuring AI adoption and capability across occupations, finding highest adoption in finance, computer science, and arts sectors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Open Source Economic Index of AI Adoption and Capability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an open-source economic index to measure AI adoption and capability across various occupations. Using publicly available user interactions with large language models and occupational task data from O*NET, the index identifies finance, computer science, and arts sectors as having the highest rates of AI adoption. To assess AI capabilities, the team created benchmark scenarios based on occupational tasks and tested an AI model, Kimi-k2.5, finding that while it performs high-level workflows accurately, it often makes errors in detailed task execution.

The study combines data-driven analysis with practical testing to provide insights into how AI is integrated into different job functions. By replicating methods used by leading AI labs and grounding evaluations in standardized occupational frameworks, the research offers a transparent and replicable approach to understanding AI's impact on the workforce. The findings highlight both the potential and current limitations of AI in automating complex labor tasks across multiple industries.

To measure adoption, we develop an open-source economic index that uses publicly available user-LLM chat data and O*NET tasks to replicate studies produced by frontier AI labs, finding that occupations in the finance, computer science, and arts sectors are those with the highest adoption rates. To measure capabilities, we build a system that generates benchmark scenarios grounded in O*NET occupations, tasks, and model-context-protocol (MCP) servers. items.title: Researchers present Dot-Flik, a scalable edge AI system for distributed insect monitoring using motion-informed frame filtering and hierarchical IoT architecture, validated on low-cost hardware with real-time performance and energy savings [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dot-Flik: A Scalable Edge AI Architecture for Distributed Insect Monitoring
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Dot-Flik, a scalable edge AI system designed for distributed insect monitoring that addresses the challenges of high hardware costs, energy consumption, and dependence on centralized processing. The system uses a motion-informed frame filtering algorithm to discard irrelevant video frames at the edge, preserving insect activity without requiring deep learning on the sensing device. It also features a distributed, hierarchical IoT architecture that separates data acquisition from AI classification, enabling greater monitoring coverage and reduced central processing demands.

The system was validated through outdoor deployments on low-cost hardware, demonstrating real-time performance at 30 frames per second with significant frame reduction and energy savings. Under light wind conditions, Dot-Flik achieved 60-80% frame reduction, up to 22.6% energy savings, and supported multiple concurrent edge streams per central node. These results suggest Dot-Flik offers a practical and efficient foundation for dense, low-cost biodiversity monitoring networks in urban environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global insect population declines necessitate scalable, continuous monitoring systems, yet existing vision-based solutions remain constrained by high hardware costs, energy demands, and reliance on centralized processing or cloud connectivity. items.title: Study finds GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 suggest narrower research methods than recent arXiv papers, with significant provider bias and reduced methodological diversity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods
items.summary:
A recent study analyzed the methodological suggestions generated by large language models (LLMs) GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 when prompted with research questions extracted from 1,000 recent computer science papers on arXiv. The study compared these LLM-generated methods to the original paper methodologies, revealing that the models tend to propose a much narrower range of research methods and exhibit significant bias toward certain model providers. This narrowing effect was consistent across the different LLMs and was most pronounced in the choice of model providers, with some academic models underrepresented and others slightly overrepresented.

The researchers mapped method features from both the LLM outputs and the papers into a shared taxonomy and measured divergence across dimensions such as dataset task type and evaluation metrics. They found that the LLMs' suggestions were query-specific but filtered through a limited set of options, reducing methodological diversity compared to the broader range found in the original papers. The study highlights the risk that researchers relying solely on LLM-generated suggestions without cross-verification may inadvertently restrict their methodological approaches to a more concentrated default set.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to guide research methodology, yet their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting remain unclear. Here, we prompt GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with an LLM-extracted research question from each of 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers and compare the resulting methodology suggestions against a paper-derived experimental inventory. Since we provide only the research question, the differences we measure reflect initial suggestions and not how optimal those suggestions are. We extract structured method features from both sources, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence across multiple taxonomy dimensions including model provider, dataset task type, and evaluation metric type. The strongest imbalance appears in provider choice, with Jensen-Shannon divergence about 3-5x larger than any other taxonomy dimension. Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 percentage points, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6pp). LLMs also suggest a much narrower range of methods overall: the effective number of model entities contracts from 1,232 to 59-96, and inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) generally exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), so the distortions are largely shared across models. Popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests confirm that the outputs are query-specific responses, but filtered through a narrower set of options. Researchers who rely on LLM suggestions without cross-checking therefore risk narrowing their methodological search space toward a more concentrated default.

items.originalTitle: Neural Architecture Search for Generative Adversarial Networks: A Comprehensive Review and Critical Analysis
items.summary:
This paper reviews Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods applied to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), focusing on how NAS automates and optimizes GAN design to enhance performance, stability, and efficiency. It categorizes various NAS approaches by search strategies and evaluation metrics, highlighting the advantages of evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods in specific scenarios. The study also emphasizes the need for robust evaluation metrics beyond traditional scores and the importance of diverse datasets for assessing GAN performance.

The review identifies current limitations in NAS for GANs and suggests directions for future research to improve these techniques. By providing a structured comparison of existing NAS-GAN methods, the paper aims to guide researchers in developing more effective architectures and advancing the field of GANs.

items.title: Researchers present KG-TRACE, a neuro-symbolic framework integrating WHO mutation knowledge graph for antimicrobial resistance prediction with 92.5% symbolic coverage and 0.976 AUROC on M. tuberculosis data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KG-TRACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Mechanistic Grounding in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed KG-TRACE, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the World Health Organization's mutation knowledge graph with neural genomic models to improve antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prediction. Tested on Mycobacterium tuberculosis data, KG-TRACE achieved a high predictive accuracy with an AUROC of 0.976 for isoniazid resistance, while providing a symbolic grounding that aligns neural attributions with established biological pathways. This approach enhances interpretability by combining genomic features and knowledge graph embeddings through a trust mechanism that balances neural evidence with biological knowledge.

The framework introduces the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a metric that quantifies how well neural model explanations correspond to known biology, achieving 92.5% symbolic coverage for isoniazid-resistant cases. KG-TRACE also identifies potential multi-drug resistance co-occurrence artifacts by flagging uncertain predictions for further laboratory review. This neuro-symbolic grounding offers a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, aiming to bridge the gap between predictive performance and clinical trust in AMR diagnostics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While WGS-based AMR prediction has reached high accuracy, existing models lack a mechanism to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. We present KG-TRACE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. Unlike existing methods that learn statistical patterns in isolation, KG-TRACE fuses genomic features and RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, dynamically weighting neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid, achieving competitive accuracy while its primary value lies in symbolic grounding, not predictive uplift. More importantly, we introduce the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric that quantifies alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Our framework achieves a 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases. We demonstrate that neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust.

items.title: Researchers propose LiMoDE, a two-stage lifelong mixture-of-dynamic-experts model for robot manipulation, demonstrating improved task adaptation and knowledge transfer in simulations and real-world tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LiMoDE: Rethinking Lifelong Robot Manipulation from a Mixture-of-Dynamic-Experts Perspective
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LiMoDE, a novel two-stage lifelong mixture-of-dynamic-experts model designed to enhance robot manipulation by improving task adaptation and knowledge transfer. The approach involves a dynamic mixture of experts (MoE) structure during multi-task pre-training to capture diverse short-term manipulation skills, followed by a lifelong adaptation mechanism that combines learned and frozen experts for new tasks. This method addresses limitations in previous models that struggled with reusable skill extraction and interaction modeling.

LiMoDE was tested on both simulated lifelong learning benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, demonstrating superior performance and strong lifelong adaptation capabilities. The model achieves these improvements with only a moderate increase in trainable parameters and inference overhead, suggesting its practical viability for continuous robot learning and generalization across tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26183v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Building a generalist robot that can leverage prior knowledge for continuous task adaptation remains a significant challenge. Previous works alleviate the catastrophic forgetting problem by parameter-efficient fine-tuning for single-task adaptation. However, they fail to extract reusable skills and model the interaction with other skills effectively. Recent works try to address these issues by learning prompts. Differently, this paper presents an architectural perspective on the Lifelong Mixture of Dynamic Experts (\textit{LiMoDE}), a novel two-stage learning scheme for lifelong robot manipulation. Specifically, a dynamic MoE structure is first proposed in the multi-task pre-training stage to learn prior knowledge, where a varied number of heterogeneous experts are activated based on the motion information to address different short-term manipulations. Subsequently, in the task adaptation stage, we design a lifelong MoE adaptation mechanism % (LiMoEAM) that learns lifelong experts and dynamically combines them with frozen ones for new tasks, facilitating the knowledge transfer during adaptation. The proposed \textit{LiMoDE} is evaluated on both the simulated lifelong learning benchmark and real-world tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving superior performance and strong lifelong adaptation by introducing a moderate number of additional trainable parameters and inference overhead.

items.title: arXiv:2606.26200 presents thesis on statistical and structural approaches to algorithmic fairness addressing limitations of current paradigms in socio-technical machine learning systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Statistical and Structural Approaches to Algorithmic Fairness
items.summary:
The thesis presented in arXiv:2606.26200 explores the limitations of current algorithmic fairness paradigms in machine learning systems, which have evolved into complex socio-technical structures influencing human opportunities. It highlights how these systems often perpetuate existing structural inequalities and biases, and critiques early fairness approaches for relying on oversimplified assumptions that reduce their effectiveness in real-world contexts. The work identifies two key shortcomings: the dependence on deterministic point estimates for fairness auditing and the neglect of individuals' structural contexts in fairness assessments.

By addressing these issues, the thesis aims to advance more robust statistical and structural methods for evaluating and improving fairness in machine learning models. This approach acknowledges the embedded social dynamics and seeks to create fairness frameworks that better reflect the complexities of socio-technical environments where these algorithms operate.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern machine learning systems have outgrown their origins as isolated predictive constructs, evolving into complex socio-technical architectures that actively mediate human opportunity. As algorithms increasingly determine access to economic and social opportunities, it has become widely recognized that these systems are deeply embedded with the structural inequalities and prejudices of their environments. The field of algorithmic fairness emerged in response to the growing recognition that models optimized for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early mitigation strategies, however, rested on fragile simplifications that limited their effectiveness in complex socio-technical environments. This thesis identifies and addresses two fundamental limitations of contemporary fairness paradigms: the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as isolated entities devoid of structural context.

items.title: Researchers introduce Hankel Reduced-order Model adapters for long-context fine-tuning, showing improved performance over LoRA on Mistral-7B across multiple language and state-tracking tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SSM Adapters via Hankel Reduced-order Modeling: Injection Site Determines Task Suitability in Long-Context Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new fine-tuning method called the Hankel Reduced-order Model (HRM) adapter, which leverages state space models to improve performance on tasks requiring long-context sequence modeling. Tested on the Mistral-7B model, HRM outperformed existing low-rank adaptation (LoRA) techniques across various language and state-tracking benchmarks, including significant gains on QuALITY and QMSum tasks. The HRM adapter uses a residual module initialized through balanced truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians and enables efficient computation via an FFT-based parallel scan.

The study also explored optimal injection sites for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, finding that integrating HRM adapters into MLP blocks yields better results for sequential state accumulation tasks. Evaluations across synthetic state-tracking and character-level language modeling further demonstrated HRM's consistent superiority. Analysis of the adapter's gating mechanisms indicated its ability to effectively modulate recurrence, offering a robust alternative to traditional low-rank adaptation methods for handling long-context dependencies in sequence modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) typically targets attention projectors, its efficacy for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation remains under-explored. We examine if PEFT for such tasks can benefit from state space model (SSMs) adapters, and if MLP blocks are better injection sites. We introduce Hankel Reduced order Model (HRM) adapter, an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians. By leveraging the time-invariance of the system matrix $\bar{A}$, HRM enables an exact FFT-based parallel scan, achieving computational parity with LoRA across all context lengths. In iso-parametric evaluations on Mistral-7B (8.4M trainable parameters), HRM outperforms LoRA variants on LongBench tasks, including QuALITY (+34.8\% relative accuracy) and QMSum (+71.6\% relative ROUGE-1). HRM further demonstrates consistent superiority across 18 configurations of synthetic state-tracking (DFA, Parity) and character-level language modeling (enwik8). Gate analysis reveals that HRM adapters effectively learn to modulate recurrence, providing a robust architectural alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling.

items.title: Researchers introduce the Red Queen Gödel Machine, an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement with co-evolving evaluators that improves coding, paper reviewing, and proof grading tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Red Queen G\"odel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Red Queen Gödel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework designed for recursive self-improvement with co-evolving evaluators that adapt alongside the agents. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed evaluation criteria, the RQGM introduces controlled utility evolution, allowing evaluation standards to change over time, which enhances performance in tasks such as coding, scientific paper reviewing, and proof grading.

The RQGM operates in epochs with fixed evaluation criteria within each epoch but updates its objectives between epochs, ensuring self-improvement guarantees while adapting to evolving goals. This approach has demonstrated improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods, including higher test pass rates in coding tasks with fewer computational resources, increased acceptance rates in scientific paper writing under diverse judging panels, and improved accuracy in proof grading. Additionally, the framework addresses biases in paper reviewing by introducing adversarial objectives that balance the evaluation of AI-generated and human work.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving agents are state-of-the-art (SOTA) on agentic coding benchmarks and have recently been extended to general domains. However, their search methods generally assume a stationary evaluation criterion: a fixed verifier, benchmark, or labeled dataset that remains valid as the agent improves. This ignores a central feature of evolution: species adapt as their environments change with them. We aim to bring the same principle to recursive self-improvement, making evaluation part of the improvement loop and opening search to evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that may surpass static benchmarks. We introduce the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM makes this possible through controlled utility evolution: search is organized into epochs with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion, while the utility can be updated at epoch boundaries, so self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch as the objective evolves across them. We begin by showing that even on verifiable coding tasks, the RQGM improves test pass rate over the prior SOTA by adding a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal. This signal is cheaper and the RQGM uses 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens. We then turn to scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing and grading, where the RQGM improves performance over prior self-improving agents: co-evolved writers reach 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under a diverse agent-as-a-judge panel, while co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI-generated papers at up to 1.91x the human rate. The RQGM corrects this by introducing an adversarial objective that discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.

items.title: Researchers introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework using LLM-based design agents to automate actor-critic architecture search, outperforming baselines on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EVOM: Agentic Meta-Evolution of Actor-Critic Architectures for Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework that automates the design of actor-critic architectures in reinforcement learning using large language model (LLM)-based design agents. EVOM frames architecture search as a bi-level optimization problem, where an inner loop trains network weights with proximal policy optimization, and an outer loop iteratively refines architecture programs through meta-evolution powered by an LLM design agent. This approach is distinct in that the LLM operates solely as an architecture designer, separate from policy execution and environment interaction.

Experimental results demonstrate that EVOM outperforms manually designed architectures, LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES on the Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm that both the meta-evolution process and the LLM design agent are critical to achieving superior performance, highlighting the framework's effectiveness in automating and improving actor-critic architecture design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In actor-critic reinforcement learning, network architectures are typically manually designed. Automating this design is challenging because each candidate must be trained before evaluation, and the design space is open-ended. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework for discovering high-performance actor-critic architectures. We frame architecture search as a bi-level optimization: an inner loop trains weights via the low-fidelity proximal policy optimization (PPO), while an outer loop drives meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. Crucially, this outer loop is powered by an LLM-based design agent that operates purely as an architecture designer, completely decoupled from policy execution and environment control. Experiments reveal that EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES, delivering superior performance on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. Ablation studies validate that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are indispensable for final performance.

items.title: Researchers use small language models to augment systematic review of social-physical human-robot interaction, identifying 10% more relevant papers missed by human reviewers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Charting the Growth of Social-Physical HRI (spHRI): A Systematic Review Pipeline Augmented by Small Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have explored the use of small language models (SLMs) with fewer than 1.5 billion parameters to assist in the systematic review of social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) literature. Although these models did not match the accuracy of human reviewers, they operated much faster and identified 10.29% more relevant papers that human reviewers had missed, demonstrating their potential to augment expert review processes.

The study highlights challenges in spHRI research due to fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies, which complicate comprehensive literature synthesis. By employing an ensemble of SLMs for title and abstract screening, the researchers showed that these models can support scalable and sustainable review practices without replacing human expertise.

This approach suggests that integrating SLMs into systematic reviews can enhance the accessibility and efficiency of large-scale literature analyses, potentially benefiting fields where rapid and thorough synthesis of research is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) has grown rapidly across robotics, human-computer interaction, human-robot interaction, and haptics. Yet, fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies make systematic synthesis difficult. To support scalable review practices, we evaluated the extent to which small language models (SLMs; < 1.5B parameters) can assist with title and abstract screening for a large spHRI systematic review. While no SLMs matched human reviewers' performance, the models operated locally and screened papers orders of magnitude faster. The combined SLM ensemble identified 39 papers reviewers missed, representing 10.29% of the final relevant dataset. These results demonstrate that SLMs can augment, rather than replace, expert reviewers and make large-scale literature reviews accessible and sustainable.

items.title: Researchers introduce SOLAR, an AI-powered framework that automatically derives validated Speed-of-Light performance bounds from PyTorch and JAX code for deep learning model optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SOLAR: AI-Powered Speed-of-Light Performance Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SOLAR, an AI-powered framework that automatically derives validated Speed-of-Light (SOL) performance bounds from PyTorch and JAX code to optimize deep learning models. SOLAR addresses the challenge of manually computing theoretical minimum execution times on target hardware by translating source programs into an intermediate representation and analytically calculating SOL bounds, ensuring comprehensive operator coverage and validated results without violations.

The framework combines a large language model frontend with deterministic processes to convert code into an affine loop intermediate representation, which is then transformed into an einsum graph for analysis. Evaluations on various benchmarks and workloads demonstrate SOLAR's ability to provide multi-fidelity performance analysis, identify optimization opportunities, support cross-platform exploration, and assist in hardware provisioning decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How fast could a deep-learning model run on target hardware, and how far is today's implementation from that limit? These questions are central to software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations. Speed-of-Light (SOL) analysis answers them by computing a workload's theoretical minimum execution time on a given architecture. Yet deriving SOL bounds remains manual, error-prone, and disconnected from rapid model development. To close this gap, we introduce SOLAR, a framework that automatically derives validated SOL bounds from PyTorch and JAX source code. SOLAR leverages both generative and deterministic components in its flow: an LLM frontend translates any source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR, validated by output comparison; a deterministic flow lifts the IR into an einsum graph; and an analytical backend computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. SOLAR provides comprehensive operator and language coverage, produces validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and offers multi-fidelity analysis that tightens bounds and surfaces optimization insights. We evaluate SOLAR across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads. These experiments demonstrate four use cases: headroom analysis at multiple fidelity levels, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

All formal proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4. This architecture is deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI.

items.title: Researchers introduce ConflictScore, a metric to measure how language models handle conflicting evidence using ConflictBench benchmark and improve truthfulness on TruthfulQA [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ConflictScore: Identifying and Measuring How Language Models Handle Conflicting Evidence
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ConflictScore, a new metric designed to evaluate how well language models recognize and handle conflicting evidence within their source documents. Unlike existing metrics that only assess whether an answer is supported or contradicted, ConflictScore measures the presence and balance of conflicting claims by breaking down responses into atomic claims and labeling them against grounding documents. This approach is supported by ConflictBench, a benchmark that includes various types of conflicts such as ambiguity and divergent opinions.

The ConflictScore framework includes two measures: ConflictScore-Count, which reflects the proportion of claims with conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio, which indicates the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. Experiments demonstrate that ConflictScore effectively identifies overconfident claims across different domains and can be used as feedback to improve the truthfulness of language models, as shown in tests on the TruthfulQA dataset.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing metrics for factuality and faithfulness evaluate whether an answer is supported or contradicted by its grounding documents, but they fail to capture when both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. We introduce ConflictScore, a novel metric that quantifies how well a model's response acknowledges conflicting evidence in its grounding documents. Our framework decomposes responses into atomic claims, labels each claim against each grounding document, and then aggregates these labels into two complementary measures: ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. We develop ConflictBench, a benchmark covering diverse forms of conflicts such as ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions, to systematically evaluate our metric. Experiments show that ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains and can serve as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA.

items.title: ProvenAI introduces a framework for measuring answer correctness, citation fidelity, and source influence in multi-hop question answering using 7,405 HotpotQA examples [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ProvenAI: Provenance-Native Traces of Evidence in Generated Answers
items.summary:
ProvenAI is a new framework designed to enhance transparency in multi-hop question answering by independently measuring three key aspects: answer correctness, citation fidelity, and the influence of each source document. Applied to the HotpotQA benchmark, ProvenAI processes 7,405 validation examples through a detailed pipeline that includes data normalization, retrieval indexing, and influence estimation. The system achieved 53.53% answer accuracy and a citation-fidelity score of 71.55%, revealing a notable citation-influence gap where some cited sources had minimal impact while uncited sources significantly influenced the output.

The framework is grounded in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, formalizing the relationship between citation audits and token-level influence measures. ProvenAI highlights the need for distinct, traceable links among retrieved, cited, and behaviorally influential evidence to ensure meaningful transparency in retrieval-augmented question answering systems. This approach also aligns with emerging cryptographic provenance methods in autonomous scientific discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented systems routinely present citations alongside generated answers, yet a citation does not confirm that the corresponding source meaningfully shaped the output. This paper introduces ProvenAI, a framework that decomposes transparency in multi-hop question answering into three independently measurable layers: answer correctness, citation fidelity against benchmark supporting evidence, and per-document influence under leave-one-resource-out intervention. Targeting the HotpotQA distractor benchmark through a seven-stage pipeline covering data normalisation, retrieval indexing, citation-aware answer generation, attribution auditing, ablation-based influence estimation, batch evaluation, and interactive inspection, ProvenAI evaluates 7,405 validation examples drawn from a canonical corpus of 509,300 passages. The system achieves 53.53% answer accuracy alongside a mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%, and a worked example surfaces what we call the citation-influence gap: a clean citation audit co-occurring with a profile in which one cited source registers only weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output. We formalise the relationship between the implemented surface proxy and a token-level KL-divergence target through a stated faithfulness condition, ground the framework in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, and discuss how the three measurement layers compose with cryptographic provenance architectures emerging in autonomous scientific discovery. ProvenAI establishes that meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across retrieved, cited, and behaviourally influential evidence as three distinct, independently measured layers.

items.title: Researchers present APRTrack, a hierarchical adversarial perturbation and retrieval framework for robust RGB-Event visual object tracking under partial target missing and modal degradation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Active Adversarial Perturbation-driven Associative Memory Retrieval for RGB-Event Visual Object Tracking
items.summary:
Researchers have developed APRTrack, a hierarchical adversarial perturbation and retrieval framework designed to enhance the robustness of RGB-Event visual object tracking, particularly under conditions of partial target loss and modality degradation. This approach addresses challenges in real-world environments where either RGB or event sensor data can become unreliable due to occlusion, edge truncation, or clutter, by simulating structured signal degradations and employing a hierarchical routing mechanism to prevent feature collapse during training.

APRTrack incorporates two adversarial perturbation branches that mimic full-modal failure and localized target absence, alongside a Footprint-guided Channel-calibrated Hopfield Retrieval (FCHR) module that compensates for missing historical information by evaluating retrieval confidence and calibrating the retrieval metric space. Extensive testing on multiple datasets, including FE108, COESOT, VisEvent, and FELT, demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in improving tracking performance. The researchers plan to release the source code and pre-trained models to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26455v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: RGB-Event tracking improves localization robustness by fusing RGB appearance textures and dense temporal motion cues from event sensors. While this multi-modal scheme broadens tracking applicability, real-world scenes suffer diverse structured signal degradations that hinder traditional multi-modal fusion. In harsh environments, either modality can lose reliability drastically, and targets frequently appear incomplete due to occlusion, edge truncation and foreground clutter.To tackle the above challenges, we present a hierarchical perturbation and retrieval framework tailored for RGB-Event tracking with robustness against partial target missing and modal degradation, termed APRTrack. To mimic real-world signal corruption, APRTrack constructs structured degradation via two adversarial perturbation branches at the modality and spatial levels, which separately simulate full-modal failure and localized target region absence. A hierarchical routing mechanism is designed to disentangle the training pipelines of the two perturbation types, effectively eliminating feature collapse induced by superimposed degradation constraints. Furthermore, we devise Footprint-guided Channel-calibrated Hopfield Retrieval (FCHR) for reliable historical information compensation. This module evaluates retrieval confidence based on association footprints between queries and memory banks, and calibrates the retrieval metric space prior to Hopfield matching, realizing controllable historical feature compensation bounded to target regions. Extensive experiments on FE108, COESOT, VisEvent, and FELT datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed strategies for the RGB-Event visual object tracking. The source code and pre-trained models will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenEvTracking

items.title: Researchers isolate a single crosscoder feature mediating RL-induced tool use in Qwen2.5-3B, improving tool correctness by 31% and enabling capability transfer to base models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a specific feature within the Qwen2.5-3B language model that mediates reinforcement learning (RL)-induced tool use, significantly improving the model's ability to generate correct tool calls. By isolating this feature using Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC), they achieved a 31% increase in tool correctness and enabled the transfer of this capability to the base model without retraining, a phenomenon termed "capability spillover." This discovery highlights how RL reshapes internal model representations to enable agentic behaviors and offers a method for runtime behavioral control of large language models.

The study involved a comprehensive hyperparameter sweep across 48 crosscoders, demonstrating that DFCs can concentrate RL-introduced capabilities into a minimal and steerable feature set. This approach not only enhances tool use accuracy but also allows passive transfer of these skills to frozen base models, suggesting new avenues for efficient model fine-tuning and control without extensive retraining.

items.title: Researchers present a five-arm ablation methodology for retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning in diffusion models, identifying key components affecting structured reasoning tasks like graph reachability and Sudoku [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Retrieval-Warmed Energy-Based Reasoning: A Five-Arm Ablation Methodology for Diffusion-as-Inference on Structured Reasoning Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a five-arm ablation methodology to analyze retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR) in diffusion models, focusing on structured reasoning tasks such as graph reachability and Sudoku. This approach isolates three confounded effects—class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse—using a diagnostic decomposition adapted from large language model retrieval-augmented generation evaluation. Their findings reveal that per-graph alignment significantly improves accuracy in graph reachability tasks, while key quality is the limiting factor in Sudoku under the current setup.

The study applies this methodology to an Erdős–Rényi all-pairs reachability task, demonstrating a substantial accuracy increase when graph alignment is preserved, and shows that random initialization can degrade performance below baseline. In contrast, for Sudoku, the analysis identifies key quality as the primary bottleneck, highlighting different components affecting performance across tasks. This work advances understanding of failure modes in iterative diffusion samplers and contributes to explainability in structured and spatio-temporal reasoning models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate iterative inference, but it is rarely clear which part of the pipeline carries the gain. We study \textbf{retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR)} -- an IRED energy-based diffusion model \cite{du2024ired} augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory -- and contribute a \textbf{five-arm ablation methodology} (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) that separates three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The diagnostic decomposition is adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation \cite{ru2024ragchecker}. On \textbf{connectivity-2} (Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi all-pairs reachability), the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches \textbf{$+35$\,pp} balanced accuracy on a fixed 1{,}000-graph validation-set diagnostic, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed, only per-graph alignment destroyed, while per-query random initialisation falls below cold -- per-graph alignment, not bias shift or stochasticity, dominates. Yet the \emph{deployable} cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. The same diagnostic logic, stopped at the key-quality screen, applied to \textbf{Sudoku} with a task-specific key encoder produces a clean negative at a \emph{different} component -- key quality, under the current setup. The decomposition names the first blocking component on each task. The setting -- graph reachability refined by an iterative diffusion sampler, with explainability of failure modes as the lens -- places the work within structured and spatio-temporal reasoning.

items.title: Researchers propose TempoWave multi-wavelet digit embeddings to improve large language model time series forecasting, achieving new state-of-the-art results across five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Speaking Numbers to LLMs: Multi-Wavelet Number Embeddings for Time Series Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TempoWave, a novel multi-wavelet digit embedding method designed to enhance large language models (LLMs) for time series forecasting. TempoWave transforms scalar numerical observations into digit-wise embeddings using multi-scale wavelet coefficients, improving the alignment between continuous numerical data and the discrete tokenization processes of LLMs. This approach preserves numerical precision and digit identity while capturing both local fluctuations and global patterns in a form compatible with transformer architectures.

Testing TempoWave across five context-rich forecasting benchmarks demonstrated consistent improvements over traditional numeric tokenization and other embedding techniques, setting new state-of-the-art performance levels. The findings highlight the importance of the numeric interface in LLM-based forecasting and suggest that multi-resolution embeddings can better integrate contextual reasoning with accurate numerical prediction. The researchers have made their code and model publicly available for further exploration and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive for context-aware time series forecasting because they can integrate heterogeneous textual signals, yet their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding interfaces are misaligned with continuous numerical values, often harming numerical ordering and forecasting reliability. We propose TempoWave, a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings constructed from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients. By directly overriding standard token representations, TempoWave seamlessly exposes both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form, ensuring that precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to common normalization operations are maintained throughout the LLM pipeline. Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving a new state-of-the-art. These results highlight the numeric interface as a key bottleneck and suggest that principled multi-resolution embeddings can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning with precise forecasting. Our code is available at https://github.com/DC-research/TempoWAVE and our model can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/Melady/TempoWAVE.

items.title: Researchers identify a 0.190 accuracy gap in fault diagnosis of deep learning programs between within-program evaluation and unseen program deployment using DynFault dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluation-Strategy Gap in Fault Diagnosis of Deep Learning Programs
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a significant accuracy gap of 0.190 in fault diagnosis of deep learning (DL) programs when comparing within-program evaluation to deployment on previously unseen programs. Using the DynFault dataset, which includes 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs, the study highlights that common diagnostic techniques perform notably worse on new programs than on those seen during training. This gap is attributed to program-level structural differences in the features used for diagnosis.

The study further examines two types of runtime features—curvature and optimizer features—and their effectiveness in diagnosing faults on unseen programs. Findings indicate that curvature features remain useful for detecting instability in new programs, whereas optimizer and activation features primarily aid diagnosis only for programs included in the training data. These insights emphasize the need for improved diagnostic methods that generalize better across different DL programs.
