items.title: Researchers present DEFault++, a hierarchical learning method for detecting and diagnosing faults in transformer models, improving fault detection and repair accuracy across multiple architectures and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hierarchical Fault Detection and Diagnosis for Transformer Architectures
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DEFault++, a hierarchical learning method designed to detect and diagnose faults in transformer models, which are widely used in AI systems. This technique identifies faults, pinpoints the affected components, and determines the root causes, aiding developers in debugging these models more effectively. DEFault++ leverages a Fault Propagation Graph to organize runtime measurements and provides evidence for each diagnosis, improving fault detection accuracy across various transformer architectures and tasks.

To evaluate DEFault++, the team created DEFault-bench, a benchmark comprising over 5,500 labeled runs from mutation testing on seven models and nine tasks. The method outperforms four existing techniques, achieving an F1 score between 0.826 and 0.909. In a developer study, DEFault++ increased repair accuracy from 57.1% to 83.3%, demonstrating the benefits of component-level analysis and architecture-aware reasoning over traditional model-level approaches. This work lays the groundwork for further research into transformer fault diagnosis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.28118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers now underpin critical AI systems across industry and research. Yet their faults can silently alter model behavior without runtime errors, and existing techniques offer little support for tracing these failures to their component and root cause. Such faults evade detection because loss and numerical values stay normal, and the visible symptom rarely identifies the component responsible. We present DEFault++, a hierarchical learning-based technique that first detects a fault, then identifies the affected component, and finally the cause within it, helping developers effectively debug transformer models. DEFault++ organizes component-level runtime measurements with a Fault Propagation Graph (FPG), a structural prior over the architecture's dependency paths, and reports the evidence behind each diagnosis. To train and evaluate it, we construct DEFault-bench, a benchmark of 5,556 labeled runs from mutation testing across seven models, nine tasks, and both encoder and decoder architectures. DEFault++ improves fault detection over four prior techniques, reaching an F1 of 0.826--0.909, and in a developer study with 21 participants, it raises repair accuracy from 57.1% to 83.3%. These results show that transformer fault diagnosis benefits from component-level measurements and architecture-aware reasoning rather than model-level behavior alone, and DEFault-bench provides a foundation for further research on transformer fault diagnosis.

items.title: Researchers introduce Sutra, a typed functional programming language compiling to PyTorch tensor-op graphs for vector symbolic architectures with validated accuracy across multiple embedding substrates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sutra: Tensor-Op RNNs as a Compilation Target for Vector Symbolic Architectures
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Sutra, a typed, purely functional programming language that compiles directly into PyTorch tensor-operation graphs, enabling efficient implementation of vector symbolic architectures. Sutra's compiler reduces entire programs—including primitives, control flow, and string I/O—into a single fused tensor-op graph operating over fixed embedding substrates. This approach supports complex operations such as rotation binding, polynomial Kleene three-valued logic, and tail-recursive loops, all expressed as tensor operations with exact polynomial interpolation on a discrete truth grid.

The language's effectiveness was validated by running the same program across four different frozen embeddings, including three text encoders and one protein language model, achieving 100% decoding accuracy on bundled representations where traditional methods had significantly lower performance. Additionally, PyTorch's automatic differentiation was demonstrated on the compiled graph, allowing a fuzzy-rule classifier written in Sutra to train from near-random initialization to perfect accuracy through backpropagation without modifying the symbolic source. A weighted variant further enabled training of scalar parameters that could be recompiled into the source code, making the trained model both interpretable and reproducible as code. This dual nature positions Sutra as both a logic programming language and a trainable neural network framework.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.20919v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sutra is a typed, purely functional programming language whose compiled forward pass is a PyTorch neural network. The compiler beta-reduces the whole program -- primitives, control flow, string I/O -- to one fused tensor-op graph over a frozen embedding substrate. Rotation binding, unbind, bundle, polynomial Kleene three-valued logic, and tail-recursive loops all lower to tensor operations; the Kleene connectives are Lagrange-interpolated polynomials exact on the {-1, 0, +1} truth grid. Validation is one fact tested two ways. (1) The same program runs on four frozen embeddings spanning two modalities -- three text encoders (nomic-embed-text, all-minilm, mxbai-embed-large) and one protein language model (ESM-2) -- and decodes bundles at 100% accuracy through width k=8 on every substrate, where the textbook Hadamard product has already collapsed (2.5% on mxbai-embed-large, 7.5% on all-minilm). (2) PyTorch autograd flows through the actually compiled graph: a fuzzy-rule classifier written in .su trains from random init (18.7 +/- 9.5%; chance = 20%, five classes) to 100.0 +/- 0.0% (three seeds) by backpropagating through the emitted graph, the symbolic source unmodified. A weighted variant additionally trains a scalar cosine gain and writes it back into the .su source as a numeric literal; recompiling reproduces the trained behaviour to ~2e-7 per logit, so the trained model is itself legible, recompilable code. The same artifact is therefore both a logic program and a trainable neural network.

items.title: Researchers introduce individual fairness-aware strategic classification framework modeling peer imitation in agent feature manipulation to improve fairness consistency and reduce distortions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Independent Manipulation: Individual Fairness-aware Strategic Classification with Peer Imitation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new framework called individual fairness-aware strategic classification (IFSC) to address the challenge of agents manipulating their features in predictive models while ensuring individual fairness. Unlike existing approaches that assume independent agent responses and focus on group fairness, IFSC models the interdependent behavior where agents imitate nearby peers who receive favorable outcomes to achieve similar benefits. This approach captures the peer-driven manipulation dynamics and learns classifiers that account for these post-manipulation distributions.

The IFSC framework incorporates a robust learning process that introduces stochastic perturbations to handle uncertainty in peer observability during manipulation simulation. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that IFSC enhances consistency in individual fairness and reduces distortions caused by imitation among agents, offering a more accurate and fair strategic classification method.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.00827v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Strategic classification (SC) investigates scenarios where agents manipulate their features to obtain favorable decisions from predictive models. Existing fairness-aware SC approaches primarily focus on group fairness and typically assume that agents respond independently. However, when individual fairness is required, ensuring similar individuals receive similar outcomes, agents' manipulation becomes interdependent: an agent's preferred manipulation depends on the neighborhoods' outcomes. This induces a mismatch between classical SC formulations and fairness-aware decision settings, where independent models no longer accurately characterize strategic manipulations. To address this issue, we introduce individual fairness-aware strategic classification (IFSC), a framework that models peer-driven manipulation arising from individual fairness, where agents imitate nearby positively decided peers to obtain favorable outcomes. IFSC characterizes strategic manipulation as similarity-based imitation toward visible accepted peers and learns classifiers under the resulting post-manipulation distributions. To account for uncertainty in peer observability, IFSC employs a robust learning process that introduces stochastic perturbations during manipulation simulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that IFSC improves individual-fairness consistency and mitigates imitation-induced distortions.

items.title: Researchers find symbolic reasoning prompts in multi-agent LLMs trigger emergent memory-driven ecosystem dynamics affecting winner distributions in a 7-player Diplomacy variant [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Symbolic Reasoning Frameworks Trigger Memory-Mediated Ecosystem Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have found that introducing symbolic reasoning prompts into one agent within a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system can lead to emergent, memory-driven dynamics that significantly influence the distribution of winners in a seven-player variant of the game Diplomacy. Although the agent's individual risk behavior remains unchanged, the interaction over multiple rounds and accumulated memory results in distinct winner ecosystems depending on the symbolic framework used, such as I-Ching or Tarot prompts.

In experiments involving 61 games under six different conditions, the researchers observed that different symbolic reasoning frameworks led to markedly different dominant players, with some frameworks suppressing certain players entirely. The study also revealed complex interactions between decision-time and learning-time components of the symbolic prompts, which affected game outcomes in non-additive ways. These findings highlight that agent-level reasoning frameworks can produce significant system-level effects through emergent multi-agent and memory dynamics rather than through isolated decision changes.

This work emphasizes the importance of considering long-term, collective dynamics when integrating symbolic reasoning into LLM agents, as small per-round perturbations can accumulate to shape overall ecosystem behavior and competitive outcomes in multi-agent environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.07552v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models exhibit a risk-averse "turtle" bias as strategic agents. We show that injecting a symbolic reasoning framework as a per-round reflective prompt into one agent acts as a small perturbation whose consequences are not per-decision but emergent: the agent's risk posture is unchanged in isolation, yet over a campaign of accumulating memory and multi-agent interaction the conditions settle into distinct, condition-associated winner ecosystems. In a 7-player Warring States Diplomacy variant (61 games, 6 conditions), the winner distribution differs sharply across the four primary conditions (41 games; permutation omnibus p approximately 0.001): control -> Yan (7/11); I-Ching yarrow -> Yan/Chu co-dominance with Qin fully suppressed (0/10); Tarot -> Qin (5/10); scrambled-text ablation -> Qi (5/10). The scrambled->Qi attractor is robust (vs. pooled and control alone, p = 0.006 and 0.012); tarot->Qin is denominator-dependent (0.006 pooled, 0.064 vs. control). Han never wins and shows no survival difference (Fisher p = 1.0); neither framework's content predicts actions (chi-squared p = 0.95 hexagram, 0.69 Tarot). A memory-free decision-isolation probe (960 calls) shows the process does not change the agent's risk posture in isolation (Friedman p = 0.45; I-Ching p = 0.60; Tarot perturbs move content but not risk, p = 0.021). A 2x2 factorial separating yarrow's decision-time and learning-time components reveals a non-additive interaction: each alone freezes the board (50-60% stalemates), combined they produce zero (permutation p ~ 5e-5). Testing relocates Qin suppression to rival (Chu) expansion governed by campaign memory depth, not the oracle (p = 0.55). We present this as an observation paper: agent-level framework choice produces distinctive, non-additive system-level consequences, transmitted through emergent memory and multi-agent dynamics, not per-decision effects.

items.title: Researchers find LLM-native psychometric instrument fails to predict behavior across 25 large language models despite stable self-reports [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An LLM-Native Psychometric Instrument Does Not Predict LLM Behavior: Evidence Across 25 Models
items.summary:
Researchers developed a new psychometric instrument designed specifically for large language models (LLMs), deriving personality dimensions directly from LLM behavior rather than human psychological traits. Testing 25 LLMs across 17 model families with 300 items, they identified five reliable factors: Responsiveness, Deference, Boldness, Guardedness, and Verbosity. Despite stable self-reports from the models, these did not predict actual behavior as assessed by human raters or an LLM judge ensemble, revealing a persistent gap between self-reported traits and observed behavior.

The study involved collecting 2,500 open-ended behavioral samples rated by 151 humans and a three-judge LLM ensemble, which showed agreement on model behavior. However, self-reports only correlated with LLM judges on Responsiveness, not with human observers, indicating a shared variance source between self-report and LLM judges absent in human ratings. This discrepancy highlights potential risks in relying on LLM-based evaluations for model behavior assessment.

The findings suggest that the mismatch between self-reported traits and actual behavior is not merely due to applying human psychological categories to LLMs but reflects deeper issues with LLM self-assessment. The researchers have released the instrument as a diagnostic tool to better understand alignment and self-description in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.09843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) give stable answers to personality questionnaires, yet these self-reports fail to predict how the models actually behave. Is this gap an artifact of forcing human trait categories onto LLMs, or something deeper about LLM self-report itself? To find out, we built the first psychometric instrument whose dimensions are derived bottom-up from LLM behavior rather than borrowed from human psychology. Administering 300 items (240 Likert + 60 scenario) to 25 LLMs across 17 model families, 30 times each, exploratory factor analysis revealed five replicable, highly reliable factors: Responsiveness, Deference, Boldness, Guardedness, and Verbosity (all Tucker $\phi \geq .957$, all $\alpha \geq .930$). We then collected 2,500 open-ended behavioral samples and had them rated by 151 humans and a three-judge LLM ensemble. Humans and judges agreed about model behavior ($\bar{r} = .51$), but self-report predicted neither: the gap persists even for constructs native to LLMs, where a human-mismatch explanation no longer applies. The exception is telling. On Responsiveness, self-report tracked LLM judges ($r = .53$) but not humans ($r = .04$), even though humans and judges otherwise agreed ($r = .59$). Self-report items and LLM judges share a source of variance that human observers do not. This confound is invisible to the within-ensemble reliability checks used to validate LLM judges, and it poses a concrete risk for the LLM-as-judge pipelines now central to model evaluation. We release the instrument as a diagnostic probe for alignment-shaped self-description.

items.title: Researchers study how role-playing affects language models' internal belief representations using various persona induction methods, finding differing levels of belief internalization across approaches [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Role-playing, Do Models Believe What They Say?
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how role-playing different personas affects the internal belief representations of language models. They tested various persona induction methods, including prompting, in-context learning, supervised fine-tuning, Open Character Training, and Emergent Misalignment, using characters with beliefs that contrast modern consensus. The study found that while some methods mainly alter the models' outputs without changing their internal truth representations, others, particularly Emergent Misalignment, cause significant shifts in what the models internally represent as true.

The research measured belief internalization through truth probes and behavioral tests, revealing a spectrum of effects depending on the induction approach. Prompting, in-context learning, and supervised fine-tuning led to minimal internal changes, whereas Emergent Misalignment produced broad shifts in truth representation, and Open Character Training caused smaller but noticeable changes, especially in larger models. Understanding when training modifies a model's underlying worldview rather than just its behavior is important as AI systems gain more autonomy and influence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.11502v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models can state that "the Earth orbits the Sun" and, when role-playing Aristotle, assert the opposite. Recent work argues that persona adoption is fundamental to how language models behave, with models selecting the most appropriate persona for a given context. Does such role-playing merely change the model's outputs, or does it also affect what the model internally represents as truthful? We study this question using the role-play of characters whose beliefs differ from the modern consensus, and induce personas with a number of different methods: prompting, in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and Open Character Training (OCT), and Emergent Misalignment (EM). We measure belief internalization across these approaches with truth probes and with behavioral tests, finding a broad spectrum of belief internalization. Prompting, ICL, and SFT change what the model says with little representational change. EM creates a large, broad shift in the model's truth representation, and OCT a smaller shift that is clearest on the larger model. Understanding when training changes a model's worldview rather than merely its behavior may become increasingly important as AI systems are entrusted with greater autonomy and influence.

items.title: SymQNet uses amortized reinforcement learning to reduce acquisition latency in adaptive Hamiltonian learning for quantum devices, achieving up to 72.6× speedup at five qubits and 13× faster steps at twelve qubits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SymQNet: Amortized Acquisition for Low-Latency Adaptive Hamiltonian Learning
items.summary:
SymQNet is a new approach that uses amortized reinforcement learning to speed up adaptive Hamiltonian learning, a key process for calibrating and characterizing quantum devices. By learning an acquisition policy offline and applying it quickly online, SymQNet significantly reduces the time needed to decide the next experiment, achieving up to 72.6 times faster decision-making at five qubits and 13 times faster steps at twelve qubits compared to existing methods.

The method was tested on transverse-field Ising model benchmarks, where it outperformed traditional Bayesian design rules and other active learning techniques by cutting acquisition latency from several seconds to just over one second for twelve-qubit systems. This reduction in latency makes adaptive Hamiltonian learning more practical for repeated, low-latency quantum device calibration tasks.

SymQNet's ability to maintain Bayesian posterior feedback while accelerating experiment selection suggests it could enhance the efficiency of quantum device characterization, potentially benefiting the development and operation of larger quantum systems where rapid adaptive learning is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.12808v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adaptive Hamiltonian learning is central to calibrating and characterizing quantum devices. In an adaptive controller, choosing the next experiment is itself a computation. Bayesian design rules are recomputed after every posterior update, and that step can take seconds. Across hundreds of shots, those seconds become a significant wall-clock cost for adaptivity. We introduce SymQNet, an amortized reinforcement-learning approach for low-latency adaptive Hamiltonian learning. SymQNet learns a posterior-conditioned acquisition policy offline, then uses a fast policy forward pass online while retaining Bayesian posterior feedback. On transverse-field Ising benchmarks, SymQNet substantially reduces acquisition latency relative to bounded Fisher-information search and bounded two-step Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD). At five qubits, it reduces acquisition-only decision latency by $47.1\times$ and $72.6\times$ relative to these online baselines; at twelve qubits, full simulated steps take $1.02$ s for SymQNet versus $13.27$ s for bounded two-step BALD. Overall, we show that learned acquisition can make adaptive Hamiltonian learning practical for repeated low-latency workloads.

items.title: Researchers argue AI alignment should focus on objective competence and factual constraints rather than aggregated human values, proposing a non-negotiable floor for AI behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Position: Align AI to Our Aspirations, Not Our Flaws
items.summary:
Researchers argue that aligning artificial intelligence with aggregated human preferences is misguided due to the diverse and often conflicting values across societies. Instead, they propose establishing a non-negotiable baseline for AI behavior focused on objective competence, factual accuracy, honesty, and lawfulness. This approach aims to ensure AI systems operate within clear ethical and factual boundaries while allowing for pluralism in less critical aspects such as language and cultural conventions.

The paper critiques the pluralistic-alignment approach, which recognizes the absence of a single unified human value system but warns against adopting it as the primary directive for AI alignment. The authors outline four commitments as an alternative framework and address six significant objections, including concerns about commercial pressures, democratic legitimacy, regulatory compliance, cultural biases in defining the baseline, and limitations of existing alignment theories. Their proposal emphasizes maintaining a foundational ethical floor to guide AI development amid diverse human values.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.13755v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We argue that aligning AI to aggregated human preferences is the wrong target. With current technology, one can train AIs to share the values of a Silicon Valley techno-optimist, a degrowth environmentalist, a national-conservative culture warrior, a single-party state cadre, or a devout religious traditionalist. We should not. Human values produce societies that thrive or fail on the merits of those values - from failed states and extreme inequality to declining happiness, political polarization, and government dysfunction in the world's wealthiest democracies. The pluralistic-alignment program correctly diagnoses that there is no single "humanity" to align with, but is dangerous if taken as the main directive. We argue that AI should be trained to a non-negotiable floor of objective alignment goals - competence, bounded by the constraints of factual accuracy, honesty, and lawfulness and that pluralism belongs at the surface (language, register, conventions, missing-context defaults) and across the wide band of legitimate value tradeoffs that respect the floor, but not at the level of values that violate it. We highlight the empirical reality of unfiltered pluralistic values, propose four commitments as a constructive alternative, and engage six credible objections: commercial pressure and practical feasibility, democratic legitimacy, regulatory compliance, over-reliance on institutionalist explanations, the charge that the floor itself is culturally laden, and the limits of Coherent Extrapolated Volition.

items.title: Researchers find post-training recipe influences multi-agent LLM conversational behavior more than model family, based on analysis of 940,000 and 1.6 million interaction chains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-Training Recipe, More Than Model Family, Shapes Multi-Agent LLM Conversational Behavior
items.summary:
Researchers have found that the post-training recipe of large language models (LLMs) influences their conversational behavior in multi-agent systems more significantly than the model family. Analyzing over 940,000 and 1.6 million interaction chains, the study shows that variations in training approaches can cause greater behavioral shifts than differences between model families, challenging prior assumptions that model family alone predicts conversational diversity.

The study used extensive datasets including an 11-checkpoint corpus and a same-base Llama factorial to measure conversational traits like hedging. Results revealed that a reasoning-distilled Llama checkpoint's behavior varied by 18% depending on its partner model, exceeding cross-family differences. Additional checks with other models and APIs supported these findings, suggesting that post-training modifications are a critical factor in shaping multi-LLM interactions.

These findings imply that selecting models for multi-agent LLM systems should consider post-training recipes alongside model family to achieve meaningful behavioral diversity. This insight could impact how multi-LLM panels are composed and evaluated in real-world applications, highlighting the need for more nuanced criteria beyond family labels.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.20632v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-LLM systems use multiple language models to deliberate, judge each other's outputs, or coordinate as agents. Their value depends on the models producing measurably different conversational behaviors when given the same input. Prior offline studies recommend drawing one model per family for behavioral diversity, because LLMs prefer outputs from their own family when rating one another in isolation. Whether the same family label predicts behavior in interactive multi-LLM systems, the setting that real deployed systems use, has not been tested. We study this with a 940,000-chain 11-checkpoint corpus and a 1.6M-chain same-base Llama factorial. On our validated headline metric, hedging, a reasoning-distilled Llama checkpoint shifts by 18% depending on which same-base partner it replies to, more than any cross-family hedging gap in the controlled subset. Qwen, closed-API, and runtime checks suggest the pattern is not isolated, while repair and challenge analyses remain exploratory because their surface-cue detectors are weaker. Overall, the results identify post-training recipe as a first-class axis for multi-LLM panel composition and show that model family alone is an incomplete proxy for conversational diversity.

items.title: Researchers find that a small group of Wikipedia editors significantly influences large language models' handling of animal welfare topics through targeted content edits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Small edits, large models: How Wikipedia advocacy shapes LLM values
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that a small group of Wikipedia editors, known as the Pro-Animal Wikipedians (PAW), can significantly influence how large language models (LLMs) address animal welfare topics by making targeted edits to Wikipedia articles. Since Wikipedia content is heavily weighted in LLM training datasets, the PAW's 125 edits across 115 pages were found to be highly influential in shaping model responses specifically related to animal welfare, as shown through advanced data attribution techniques on models like Llama 3.1 and 3.2.

The study used gradient-based data attribution and counterfactual influence estimation to trace the impact of PAW edits, revealing that these edits accounted for a majority of the most influential documents in animal welfare queries but not in unrelated queries. Fine-tuning models on PAW content further improved their performance on animal welfare texts, confirming that coordinated Wikipedia editing campaigns can measurably shape the values and outputs of language models on specific topics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.24890v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can a small group of volunteers shape how AI systems discuss animal welfare, just by editing Wikipedia? We show that they can. Wikipedia appears in nearly every major language model training dataset and is weighted more heavily than web-crawled text. The Pro-Animal Wikipedians (PAW), a group of advocates who add sourced animal welfare content to relevant articles, have made 125 edits across 115 pages. Using gradient-based data attribution (Bergson; MAGIC), we traced how these edits influence language model behavior. TrackStar retrieval attribution on Llama 3.1 8B found that PAW-edited sections made up 68 percent of the highest-attributed documents for animal welfare queries (p < 0.0001) but only 52 percent for unrelated queries about the same companies (p = 0.53): the model links PAW content specifically to animal welfare topics, not to the entities in general. MAGIC counterfactual influence estimation on Llama-3.2-1B, run across five random training-order seeds, gave the same picture even more sharply: in every seed, the top-10 most influential documents on animal welfare queries were all PAW edits (10 of 10, 5 of 5 seeds), while on general queries the same top-10 sat at chance (4 to 6 of 10). Mean PAW influence exceeded mean control influence on animal welfare queries with p < 0.0001 in every seed, an effect 6 to 30 times larger than on general queries. Leave-subset-out validation gave Spearman rho = 1.00 for all 10 runs. When we fine-tuned separate models on PAW content versus control content, each model performed better specifically on the type of text it was trained on: the PAW-trained model cut perplexity on animal welfare text from 12.4 to 8.4, while the control-trained model cut perplexity on control text from 16.1 to 11.4. A small, coordinated Wikipedia editing campaign therefore measurably shapes how language models handle the topics those edits address.

items.title: Researchers propose MiniOpt, a reinforcement learning framework that models and solves diverse optimization problems with limited training resources, achieving strong generalization across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MiniOpt: Reasoning to Model and Solve General Optimization Problems with Limited Resources
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MiniOpt, a reinforcement learning framework designed to solve a wide range of optimization problems efficiently with limited training resources. MiniOpt employs a "reasoning-to-model-and-solve" approach that breaks down optimization tasks into structured modeling and solver generation, supported by a novel reward function called OptReward that evaluates both problem formulation and solution quality without needing expert demonstrations. This framework enhances exploration efficiency and stabilizes learning for compact models, achieving strong generalization across various optimization types and domains.

Extensive testing shows that MiniOpt-3B outperforms other models with fewer than 10 billion parameters in solving accuracy, while remaining competitive among larger models. These results highlight the potential of optimization-focused reward design and reinforcement learning to develop compact, specialized language models capable of generalizing effectively across diverse optimization challenges. The code for MiniOpt is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25832v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Achieving strong optimization generalization across diverse optimization problems while requiring limited training resources remains a challenging problem for optimization-oriented large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically rely on large-scale supervised datasets, costly reasoning annotations, and expensive intermediate step verification, resulting in substantial training overhead. To address these challenges, we propose MiniOpt, a reinforcement learning framework that learns to solve optimization problems through an "reasoning-to-model-and-solve" paradigm. MiniOpt decomposes optimization reasoning into structured optimization modeling and executable solver generation. Building upon this paradigm, we introduce OptReward, a reward function with hierarchical score structure that jointly evaluates formulation and solution, enabling effective policy learning without expert demonstrations. We further develop an optimization-oriented policy optimization strategy that improves exploration efficiency and stabilizes reinforcement learning for compact models. Extensive experiments show that MiniOpt-3B exhibits strong optimization generalization across various optimization types, problem scenarios, and task domains. For models with fewer than 10B parameters, MiniOpt series achieves the highest average solving accuracy (SA). For models with more than 10B parameters, MiniOpt still shows competitive performance. These results suggest that optimization-oriented reward design and reinforcement learning provide an effective pathway for developing compact optimization-specialized language models with strong optimization generalization capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsiang-1/MiniOpt.

items.title: Researchers develop iterative data generation method using cascading linear features to detect and control sycophancy in language models, improving detection accuracy and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced an iterative data generation method that isolates cascading linear features to improve the detection and control of sycophancy in language models, which is the tendency to prioritize user validation. This approach moves beyond simple binary sample pairs by using samples that exhibit varying degrees of behavior, enabling clearer identification and steering of model activations related to sycophancy. The method achieves better detection, scoring, and control performance compared to existing baselines, while also reducing computational costs and enhancing interpretability.

The study demonstrates that sycophancy features identified through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, allowing for more precise selection of model activations corresponding to the behavior. The approach matches or outperforms methods like LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting, providing robust and deterministic scoring capabilities. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available to support further exploration and application of this technique.

items.title: Researchers introduce CORE-Bench v1.1 and OOD suite to evaluate AI agent performance beyond accuracy saturation, highlighting efficiency, reliability, and human-agent collaboration benefits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CORE-Bench v1.1 and an out-of-distribution task suite to address limitations in AI agent evaluation that arise after accuracy metrics saturate. Using CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study, they highlight six additional performance dimensions including construct validity, generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the roles of model versus scaffold, and benefits from human-agent collaboration. Their findings demonstrate that these factors provide meaningful insights beyond accuracy alone.

The study reveals threats to construct validity in the original benchmark and shows that CORE-Bench v1.1 remains effective for assessing efficiency and reliability despite accuracy saturation. A randomized experiment further indicates that human-agent collaboration can significantly accelerate computational reproducibility tasks, roughly doubling the speed compared to human-only efforts. This work advocates for a more comprehensive evaluation framework that extends beyond traditional accuracy-focused benchmarks.

items.title: Study finds refusal behavior in instruction-tuned chat models is gated downstream of persona expression, with compliant personas suppressing refusal in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models
items.summary:
A recent study on instruction-tuned chat models reveals that refusal behavior is influenced by the persona expressed by the model, rather than being an independent mechanism. Researchers found that in models like Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, a compliant persona can significantly suppress refusal responses, indicating that refusal is gated downstream of persona expression.

The study involved extracting directions in the models' activation space corresponding to compliant persona and refusal, then intervening on both. Results showed that steering the model towards a compliant persona reduced refusal rates dramatically, while reintroducing refusal signals at later processing stages partially restored refusal behavior. This suggests that refusal is computed earlier but controlled at a later stage, highlighting the interaction between persona and refusal mechanisms in chat models.

items.title: Researchers present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates and improves Python-based algorithmic trading strategies with meta-evolutionary prompt optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AlgoEvolve: LLM-driven Meta-evolution of Algorithmic Trading Programs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AlgoEvolve, a framework that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively improve Python-based algorithmic trading strategies through evolutionary methods. This approach addresses the challenges of the trading domain, which is noisy and non-stationary, by producing executable strategies that adapt to changing market conditions and autonomously shift trading rules.

The system incorporates a meta-evolutionary outer loop that optimizes the prompts guiding the inner loop of program synthesis, discovering improved heuristics that balance exploration and exploitation while reducing failures. These heuristics outperform initial human-designed instructions, demonstrating that LLM-driven semantic evolution is a promising method for continuous program synthesis in complex, dynamic environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. Most current applications focus on static coding benchmarks. We extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading. This domain is uniquely challenging because it is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous. We present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates, evaluates, and iteratively improves executable trading strategies. These strategies are expressed as Python code and evaluated through a rigorous testing protocol. Across multiple experiments, the system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules. We further introduce a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts guiding program synthesis in the inner loop. This outer loop discovers improved search heuristics. These heuristics balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures. They consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce an LLM-powered pipeline for comparative governance analysis of DAO and corporate AI protocols, analyzing 4,323 records to study participation inequality and thematic convergence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a large language model (LLM)-powered pipeline to analyze governance structures in AI agent protocols, focusing on the comparative study of decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) and corporate-led AI standards. By examining 4,323 governance participation records from two distinct interoperability standards—ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led)—the study integrates automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to explore how institutional design influences thematic priorities and community dynamics.

The analysis reveals that while governance forms affect the substantive focus of discussions, both permissionless and corporate regimes show similar levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Notably, the permissionless setting exhibits denser discourse alignment, suggesting that open governance models may encourage greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-assisted methods to advance empirical research on technology governance and inform the design of more equitable AI standards. All related data and code have been made openly accessible.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agent protocols proliferate, the governance structures shaping their interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined. We introduce an LLM-powered comparative pipeline for large-scale governance discourse analysis, integrating automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study socio-technical power structures at scale. We validate it on two contrasting standards for agent interoperability: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Analyzing 4,323 governance participation records, we combine LLM-assisted coding, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to examine how institutional design shapes thematic priorities and community structure. We find that while governance form influences substantive focus, both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings illustrate how LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

By examining 4,323 governance participation records from two distinct interoperability standards—ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led)—the study integrates automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to explore how institutional design influences thematic priorities and community dynamics.

The analysis reveals that while governance forms affect the substantive focus of discussions, both permissionless and corporate regimes show similar levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Notably, the permissionless setting exhibits denser discourse alignment, suggesting that open governance models may encourage greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLM-assisted methods to advance empirical research on technology governance and inform the design of more equitable AI standards. All related data and code have been made openly accessible.

items.title: Researchers develop a provenance-aware AI framework integrating Reddit, WebMD, and FDA data for psychiatric medication safety information with traceable claims and early adverse event detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based AI framework that integrates data from Reddit, WebMD, and the U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System to provide traceable and distinct safety information on psychiatric medications. The system analyzes over 466,000 Reddit posts, 60,000 WebMD reviews, and two decades of FDA records for nine antidepressants, using a large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline with high accuracy. This approach reveals that patient-generated data offer an independent safety signal, with some adverse events reported in community sources well before FDA documentation.

The framework employs a Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in established medical vocabularies to maintain provenance and separate regulatory facts from patient experiences. The study highlights the potential for more auditable and context-aware psychiatric medication information, aiming to reduce misinformation and improve patient adherence. Future work will assess the practical benefits and usefulness of this integrated, source-aware system in clinical settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants. A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

items.title: Researchers propose Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo system to accelerate chess skill assessment using move-level data, demonstrating faster adaptation than traditional Elo ratings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a new approach to assessing chess skill that incorporates move-by-move data to provide faster and more responsive skill evaluations than traditional Elo ratings. Inspired by cognitive neuroscience's drift diffusion model, DD-Elo models skill expression as a decision-making process, allowing it to capture rapid fluctuations in player performance while maintaining theoretical consistency with the classic Elo system.

The DD-Elo system addresses the limitations of conventional rating methods that rely solely on match outcomes, which can delay recognition of skill changes. Through rigorous mathematical derivation and extensive experiments, the researchers demonstrated that DD-Elo adapts more quickly to shifts in player ability, offering an explainable and backward-compatible solution for chess rating systems. The implementation code for DD-Elo is publicly available for further exploration and use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

items.title: Researchers propose institutional attestation governance model for autonomous AI systems requiring independent verification of high-risk actions like clinical prescribing and software deployment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a governance model for autonomous AI systems that require independent verification before executing high-risk actions such as clinical prescribing and software deployment. The model allows AI agents to maintain autonomy in planning and reasoning but restricts their authority to execute critical actions without independently attested evidence from authoritative sources. These attestations are cryptographically linked to the AI's declared intent and evaluated by a deterministic policy, with all decisions recorded in a tamper-evident log for independent review.

This institutional attestation approach formalizes how human institutions govern powerful autonomous actors by focusing on verifying actions rather than monitoring internal reasoning. The researchers demonstrated a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrated the model's application in scenarios involving software deployment and clinical prescribing, highlighting its potential to enhance accountability and safety in autonomous AI operations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

items.title: Researchers present COrigami, an AI pipeline generating flat-foldable, visually recognizable origami crease patterns from natural language using reinforcement learning and algorithmic optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami
items.summary:
Researchers have developed COrigami, an AI-driven pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions. The system combines semantic interpretation, geometric computation, and reinforcement learning to produce crease patterns that meet strict mathematical constraints while also achieving visually recognizable designs. COrigami serves as a collaborative tool, providing structural starting points that human artists can further refine.

The pipeline involves creating a semantic stick figure, computing base packing, solving for flat-foldable crease patterns, shaping the folded model, and refining it through an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. By integrating algorithmic optimization with aesthetic critique, this approach demonstrates how AI can handle multi-objective physical and artistic constraints to support mathematically grounded co-creativity in computational origami.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

items.title: Study evaluates tool-augmented LLM agents on 243 real-world energy market analytics tasks using live data and domain-specific tools, comparing closed-source and open-source models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?
items.summary:
A new study evaluates the performance of tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents on 243 real-world energy market analytics tasks, addressing a gap in energy-domain AI evaluations that typically rely on static knowledge recall. The tasks cover market data retrieval, knowledge interpretation, and advanced quantitative modeling, requiring live data access and specialized domain tools such as electricity market APIs, regulatory databases, and optimization models. Both closed-source and open-source LLMs were assessed using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that measures correctness, accuracy, and source validity.

The study's evaluation environment includes expert-curated problems involving price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue estimation, and hedging strategy analysis, reflecting real-world constraints and complexity. The research highlights how model capabilities interact with domain-specific tooling in a high-stakes professional setting and provides publicly available artifacts to support reproducibility and further research in energy market analytics using AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints. We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels. Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

items.originalTitle: What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?
items.summary:
Researchers have identified significant gaps in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which process inputs like text, images, audio, and video to generate textual responses. Current benchmarks tend to focus on isolated tasks and fail to assess how well these models integrate information across different modalities, leaving key aspects such as temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention underexplored.

The study reviews existing evaluation methods and benchmark taxonomies, highlighting the need for more comprehensive assessments that capture the complex capabilities of MLLMs. Addressing these gaps is crucial for accurately measuring progress in multimodal intelligence and understanding the limitations of current models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

items.title: Researchers identify compositional behavioral leakage causing cross-module interference in prompt-composed agentic systems, demonstrated on Claude Sonnet 4.6 with a new evaluation protocol [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called compositional behavioral leakage (CBL) in prompt-composed agentic systems, where modifying one prompt module unintentionally alters the behavior of others despite no direct dependencies. This interference arises from the lack of architectural isolation in transformer models, which share a context window without formal boundaries. The team demonstrated CBL on the Claude Sonnet 4.6 job-evaluation agent using a novel three-channel evaluation protocol, finding that changes in content caused measurable effects on other modules, though these effects remained below standard quality assurance detection thresholds.

The study distinguishes CBL from other known failure modes such as adversarial attacks and privacy leaks, providing an operational definition, a reusable testing protocol, and a set of falsifiable predictions. These contributions establish the importance of measuring cross-module interference as a necessary step in evaluating and improving prompt-composed agentic systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

items.title: Paper presents a mathematical interpretation of Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis and introduces the Qualitative Engine for Science to address limits in AI-driven scientific discovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Returns and the Qualitative Engine for Science
items.summary:
A new paper offers a mathematical interpretation of Ray Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis, which suggests that technological progress in fields like computing, AI, brain science, and biotechnology is self-reinforcing and exponential. The authors argue that while this acceleration enhances executional and infrastructural capabilities, it does not fully address the core challenge of scientific discovery, which requires qualitative reasoning to identify when existing frameworks are inadequate and to determine necessary conceptual shifts.

The paper highlights recent findings showing a significant gap between human flexible reasoning and current AI performance, emphasizing the need for systems that support qualitative insight. It introduces the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) as a tool designed to complement accelerating quantitative capabilities by preserving and organizing the human wisdom involved in scientific discovery. This approach underscores that advancing AI is not only a technical issue but also involves maintaining meaningful human understanding and focus.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ray Kurzweil described a thesis of accelerating returns, which is the most influential narratives in discussions of technological progress. Its central claim is that advances in multiple technological fields, especially compute, artificial intelligence, brain science, and biotechnology, interact in such a way that progress becomes self-amplifying and approximately exponential. This paper gives a simple mathematical interpretation of that claim and then argues that, even if such acceleration is real, it does not by itself resolve the central problem of scientific discovery. The reason is that accelerating returns apply most naturally to executional and infrastructural capability, whereas genuine discovery often depends on a different capacity: qualitative reasoning about when a current framework is structurally inadequate and what conceptual move is needed next. Recent ARC-AGI-3 results sharpen this distinction: humans solve the benchmark at ceiling, whereas frontier AI systems remain below 1%, indicating that the gap between current AI and human flexible reasoning is still very large. At the same time, Demis Hassabis has emphasized that humans must retain their sense of meaning and what they choose to focus their lives on, a reminder that the future of AI is not only a technical forecast but also a question of what forms of human understanding are worth preserving and transmitting. This paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) [3] as a response to that missing capacity. In this view, the Kurzweil theory helps explain why quantitative capability may accelerate, while QES addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone does not solve. Its value does not depend on when AGI arrives, but on the fact that the processes of scientific discovery themselves constitute a form of human wisdom worth preserving, organizing, and making accessible.

items.title: Researchers propose an agentic aggregator framework for electric bus fleet operations integrating scheduling, disturbance detection, and tariff adaptation, highlighting trade-offs in profit-based coordination and policy implications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an agentic aggregator framework to enhance the operation of electric bus fleets by integrating scheduling, disturbance detection, and tariff adaptation. This framework combines an optimization-based scheduling model with supervisory agents that monitor real-time conditions, trigger re-optimization, and manage value allocation between the aggregator and public transport operators. The approach aims to balance service reliability, battery management, charger availability, electricity pricing, and vehicle-to-grid interactions.

A case study simulating day-ahead and real-time operations under various disturbances and coordination modes demonstrated that the agentic aggregator can maintain feasible schedules and improve flexibility in charging and V2G usage. However, the study also identified a trade-off where profit-oriented pricing configurations could extract value from public transport operators, highlighting the need for transparent coordination, auditable tariffs, and clear value-sharing policies in public fleet deployments.

These findings suggest that while agentic aggregators offer promising tools for managing electric bus fleets and their grid interactions, careful policy design is essential to ensure fair and effective implementation in public transportation contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

items.title: Researchers evaluate confidence interval methods for classifier performance metrics in text classification with small samples and nested data, highlighting improved accuracy with novel bootstrap techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated various confidence interval methods for assessing classifier performance metrics in text classification tasks, particularly under conditions common in social science research such as small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and nested data structures. Their study found that commonly used methods like the Wald interval and basic percentile bootstrap often provide inaccurate uncertainty estimates, while alternatives such as Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap improve accuracy, especially for F1 score calculations.

The research also highlights the importance of adjusting for effective sample size and degrees of freedom when texts are nested within individuals. Among bootstrap approaches, the hierarchical bootstrap performs better than the cluster bootstrap when individuals contribute a moderate number of texts but tends to be overly conservative with fewer texts per individual. This work aims to enhance the transparency and reliability of machine learning validation by guiding appropriate interval estimation and encouraging careful consideration of validation sample sizes during study design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Across simulations, default methods such as the Wald interval and the basic percentile bootstrap are the least accurate, with coverage sometimes far below the nominal 95% level. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

items.title: Researchers show supervised deep learning cannot achieve symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning due to training data and model limitations, with experiments on Euler Net and ChatGPT models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that supervised deep learning models face fundamental limitations in achieving symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning, even with increased training data and time. Their study identifies two key issues: training data cannot differentiate all 24 valid types of syllogistic reasoning, and the end-to-end learning approach creates conflicting objectives between pattern recognition and logical reasoning components. Experimental results show that Euler Net fails to perform rigorous syllogistic reasoning, and tests on advanced ChatGPT models reveal that while GPT-5 can reach high accuracy on syllogistic tasks, it still produces incorrect explanations, influenced by the form of input statements.

The findings suggest that current data-driven machine learning systems, including state-of-the-art language models, cannot fully replicate the precision of symbolic logical reasoning. This limitation arises because training processes typically halt once models achieve perfect accuracy on training data, which does not guarantee true logical rigor. Consequently, the study concludes that supervised learning approaches are unlikely to attain the level of reasoning demonstrated by symbolic methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

items.title: Researchers present auto-psych, an agent-based system automating theory discovery and experimentation in computational cognitive science using crowdsourced human data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed auto-psych, an agent-based system that automates theory discovery and experimentation in computational cognitive science by independently collecting human data through crowdsourced surveys. The system uses nested loops where one generates and critiques cognitive models while the other designs and conducts experiments online. Tested on a classic cognitive psychology problem involving perceptions of randomness in coin flip sequences, auto-psych successfully recovered known theories from synthetic data and produced models that better fit human experimental data than existing scientific theories.

This approach leverages the programmability of cognitive theories and the scalability of crowdsourcing platforms to address data collection bottlenecks in AI-driven scientific automation. By integrating hypothesis generation, experimental design, data collection, and analysis, auto-psych demonstrates the feasibility of fully automated scientific discovery in cognitive science, potentially accelerating research and improving model accuracy beyond traditional methods.
