items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

items.title: arXiv paper reviews external validity indexes for clustering evaluation with ground truth, recommending centroid index for cluster-level and pair-set index for point-level measures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?
items.summary:
A new paper on arXiv reviews common external validity indexes used for evaluating clustering results when ground truth data is available. The authors recommend the centroid index (CI) as an intuitive and explainable cluster-level measure. For more detailed, point-level evaluation, they suggest the pair-set index (PSI), which provides a normalized score unbiased by cluster sizes, while clustering accuracy (ACC) or other set-matching measures are suitable if all points are to be weighted equally.

The paper focuses on set-matching-based measures and compares their properties to guide researchers in selecting appropriate evaluation metrics based on their specific clustering analysis needs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

items.title: Researchers present JERP, a method that jointly updates experiential rules and policies for large language model agents to improve decision-making in complex interactive tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed JERP, a method that simultaneously updates experiential rules and policies for large language model (LLM) agents to enhance decision-making in complex interactive tasks. JERP integrates a long-term rule pool with policy optimization by using interaction trajectories to both refine the rules and improve the agent's policy, ensuring alignment between the two. This approach allows the agent to retrieve relevant rules during decision-making and adapt its behavior based on past experiences.

JERP addresses limitations of previous methods that either kept experience as static natural-language rules or updated model parameters separately, which could lead to inconsistencies or limited correction in sparse-reward environments. By jointly learning from the same interaction data, JERP maintains stable and effective behaviors that evolve with the policy. Experiments on environments like AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate that JERP consistently improves decision performance for LLM agents in multi-step tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce OpenRCA 2.0 with PAVE protocol for step-wise causal supervision in root cause analysis, revealing LLMs recover exact root causes in 20.7% of cases across 11 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced OpenRCA 2.0, a new benchmark for root cause analysis (RCA) that includes step-wise causal annotations using the PAVE protocol. This approach addresses limitations in existing datasets by labeling not only the root cause but also the causal propagation path from cause to observed symptom, enabling more rigorous evaluation of large language models (LLMs) in multi-step reasoning and long-context understanding. Testing 11 advanced LLMs on OpenRCA 2.0 revealed that they correctly identify the exact root cause in only 20.7% of cases on average.

The PAVE protocol leverages fault injection interventions to reconstruct causal paths, shifting evaluation from backward symptom inference to forward cause-to-effect verification. While LLMs identified at least one correct root cause in 76.0% of cases, they grounded that cause in a verified causal path only 61.5% of the time, highlighting a significant gap in causal reasoning. This step-wise causal supervision uncovers failure modes hidden by outcome-only evaluations and is essential for developing trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

items.title: Researchers propose TOPS, a training-free visual token pruning method for multimodal large language models that removes up to 77.8% of tokens while preserving or improving performance on LLaVA-NeXT models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic method for visual token pruning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). TOPS aims to improve efficiency by removing up to 77.8% of visual tokens while maintaining or enhancing performance, as demonstrated on LLaVA-NeXT models. This approach is based on three principles—Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity—derived from an information-theoretic analysis to optimize token selection.

Extensive testing across seven MLLM architectures and fourteen benchmarks shows that TOPS outperforms existing pruning methods. Notably, it preserves full or slightly improved performance on both 7B and 13B parameter LLaVA-NeXT models despite significant token reduction. The findings suggest that eliminating redundant visual tokens can reduce hallucination and guide the development of more efficient multimodal models in the future.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

items.title: Researchers introduce process harness mechanism to add policy-governed agentic layers to legacy workflows using the Task-Decision-Flow model and CUGA FLO implementation for Agentic BPM [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a process harness mechanism that enhances legacy workflows by adding a policy-governed agentic layer without replacing the existing workflow engine. This approach, based on the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, integrates three types of agents—TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, and FlowAgent—that contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight at designated control points while maintaining the engine's structural control. The CUGA FLO implementation demonstrates this model in a loan approval workflow, balancing deterministic execution with policy-driven agentic autonomy to meet both imperative and normative process requirements.

The TDF model rigorously defines the process harness through a data schema and execution semantics, enabling large language model reasoning to be distributed across specialized agents governed by explicit policies from the process FRAME. This design allows for runtime flow adaptation and regulatory overrides, ensuring compliance and flexibility within legacy systems. The process harness thus offers a novel way to uplift existing workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) by combining structural enforcement with autonomous decision-making capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

items.title: Researchers propose GAversary, a genetic algorithm using GloVe embeddings to generate adversarial text attacks that reduce natural language model accuracy from 76.8% to 5.8% on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GAversary, a genetic algorithm that uses GloVe embeddings to create adversarial text attacks against natural language processing models. GAversary operates as a black-box method, requiring only the model's output logits to guide its search for effective word replacements. This approach significantly reduces model accuracy on benchmark datasets, dropping it from 76.8% to as low as 5.8%, outperforming existing attacks like BAE and A2T.

GAversary improves semantic similarity in adversarial examples by leveraging GloVe embeddings during mutation, although it modifies nearly twice as many words as other methods and incurs a slight increase in runtime. The method demonstrates the vulnerability of NLP models to evolutionary-generated adversarial inputs, highlighting challenges in securing deep learning systems against such attacks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

items.title: Researchers introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer with physically informed conditioning for probabilistic Earth observation forecasting, improving vegetation decline prediction under extreme weather conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer designed for probabilistic Earth observation forecasting that incorporates physically informed conditioning to better predict vegetation decline under extreme weather conditions. This model treats weather as a conditioning signal and addresses uncertainty in forecasting caused by sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. EO-WM distinguishes between climatological baselines and weather anomalies, accumulating physical stress signals over time to capture sustained heat and drought effects.

To assess the model's ability to respond accurately to changing weather, the researchers introduced two new benchmarks: the Extreme Summer Benchmark for predicting vegetation degradation severity and the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for evaluating forecast fidelity under altered weather conditions. Experiments demonstrated that EO-WM improves prediction accuracy of vegetation decline amplitude by 5.63% and directional hit rate by 7.80%, while maintaining competitive performance on standard pixel-level metrics. The model and benchmarks will be made publicly available to support further research in Earth observation forecasting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

items.originalTitle: Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation can significantly accelerate Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models compared to traditional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. By applying SBI to a COVID-19 SECIR model with intensive care unit occupancy data from Germany, they achieved comparable accuracy to MCMC while reducing computation time from thousands of seconds to under 200 seconds, leveraging GPU resources.

The study compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases, including both short 31-day inference windows and a complex 201-day reconstruction involving multiple transmission changes. SBI maintained strong agreement with MCMC in posterior distributions and predictive performance, even in the more challenging long-term scenario, while offering substantial runtime improvements.

These findings suggest that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for near-real-time Bayesian calibration of epidemiological models, facilitating faster outbreak analysis and public health decision-making during infectious disease events.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

items.title: Researchers study prompt injection in automated résumé screening with large language models, finding it boosts rankings when rare but loses effectiveness as manipulation spreads, raising fairness concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Injection in Automated R\'esum\'e Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated the impact of prompt injection—subtle self-promotional text without new qualifications—on automated résumé screening using large language models (LLMs). Their controlled experiments reveal that prompt injection can improve applicant rankings when résumé quality is similar and few candidates use this tactic, but its effectiveness declines sharply as more candidates engage in manipulation, eventually becoming ineffective when widespread. The study also finds that in cases of varied candidate quality, prompt injection is generally less effective but can sometimes allow lower-quality applicants to outrank higher-quality ones, raising concerns about fairness in algorithmic hiring.

The research highlights that LLM-based screening systems are most vulnerable to manipulation when candidate quality differences are small and prompt injection is rare. These findings underscore the challenges of maintaining fairness and reliability in automated hiring processes as candidates adapt to algorithmic evaluation methods. The authors have made their code and resources publicly available to support further study in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated r\'esum\'e screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when r\'esum\'e quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

items.title: Researchers propose language-based digital twins using large language models to mimic elderly conversational behavior for cognitive health monitoring, showing comparable accuracy to real data on I-CONECT dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language-Based Digital Twins for Elderly Cognitive Assistance
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a language-based digital twin framework that uses large language models to replicate the conversational behavior of elderly individuals, aiming to support cognitive health monitoring. By integrating stylometric features and contextual metadata, the system models individual speech patterns to detect early signs of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI). Evaluation on the I-CONECT dataset demonstrated that these digital twins maintain identity-specific traits and achieve prediction accuracy for cognitive scores comparable to real data, outperforming standard GPT-generated responses.

The approach employs a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder to assess both the quality of conversation reconstruction and cognitive score prediction, highlighting its potential as a scalable, non-invasive tool for personalized and continuous monitoring of cognitive health in older adults.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital twins have emerged as a promising paradigm for personalized healthcare, enabling modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories. In cognitive health, early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging, where language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers. In this work, we propose a language-based digital twin framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to mimic the conversational behavior of elderly individuals by incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. To evaluate fidelity and cognitive consistency, we introduce a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that jointly measures reconstruction quality and predicts cognitive scores. Experiments on the I-CONECT dataset show that the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, while outperforming baseline GPT-generated responses. These results highlight the potential of language-based digital twins as a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.

items.title: Researchers benchmark four open-weight language models on Global AI Dataset v2 to assess geographic bias and accuracy disparities across 227 countries from 2010 to 2023 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Open-Weight Foundation Models for Global AI Technical Governance
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated four open-weight large language models using the Global AI Dataset v2 to investigate geographic bias and accuracy differences across 227 countries from 2010 to 2023. The study addresses limitations of previous research by using publicly available models, focusing on data within the models' training periods, and employing a detailed five-category classification of model responses to distinguish between accurate answers, confident fabrications, and other response types.

The analysis involved approximately 2,990 observations across 18 indicators aligned with the IEEE IRAI 2026 framework, applying mixed-effects logistic regression and difference-in-differences methods to assess disparities. This approach provides a more rigorous and transparent assessment of how geographic representation in training data affects model performance in AI governance contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in artificial intelligence (AI) governance analysis across national and international organisations. There is, however, growing evidence that such models produce significantly less accurate responses for countries that are underrepresented in their training data-a pattern described in existing literature as geographic bias. Existing studies examining this phenomenon are subject to three methodological limitations that together undermine their findings: (1) reliance on proprietary systems whose weights are not publicly released, which prevents independent replication; (2) evaluation of model knowledge about years that fall after data collection for model training had concluded, leading to geographic ignorance in addition to the natural limits of each model's knowledge; and (3) use of coarse binary response classification that cannot distinguish models' confident fabrication (HF) from their honest acknowledgement of uncertainty. This study addresses all three limitations by benchmarking four open-weight frontier language models against the Global AI Dataset v2 (GAID v2), a verified ground-truth database of 24,453 indicators across 227 countries published on Harvard Dataverse in January 2026. A total of 18 indicators, mapped to the eight thematic dimensions of the IEEE IRAI 2026 framework, are selected from GAID v2, yielding approximately 2,990 country-metric-year observations across six evaluation years (within the period of 2010-2023). Model responses are classified using a five-category scheme that distinguishes (a) verified accuracy (VA), (b) HF, (c) honest refusal (HR), (d) qualitative hedging (QH), and (e) misattribution (MF). Geographic disparities in accuracy are estimated through mixed-effects logistic regression and difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis.

items.title: Paper analyzes legal and technical risks of AI-generated music under US copyright law, highlighting gaps in protection for synthesized vocal likeness and implications of recent cases and legislation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generative AI and Copyright Infringement: A Legal-Technical Analysis of AI Music Generation Systems Under 17 U.S.C. Title 17
items.summary:
This paper explores the legal and technical challenges of AI-generated music under U.S. copyright law, focusing on the use of copyrighted lyrics, AI-composed melodies, and synthetic vocals that imitate real artists. It examines whether creating and monetizing songs using protected lyrics combined with AI-generated voices or styles infringes on exclusive rights under Title 17 of the U.S. Code. The analysis highlights that unauthorized lyric use likely violates musical composition rights, while AI-generated voice imitation generally falls outside federal sound recording protections and is instead governed by state publicity laws.

The study reviews recent court cases and legislation, such as Concord v. Anthropic and Tennessee's "ELVIS Act," to illustrate the current legal landscape. It also maps AI technical components like prompt encoding and neural vocoders to associated legal risks, identifying a regulatory gap where federal law protects lyrics and melodies robustly but offers limited remedies for synthesized vocal likeness. The paper concludes with policy recommendations aimed at clarifying rules for AI music creation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has enabled users to synthesize music with text prompts, combining copyrighted lyrics, AI-composed melodies, and synthetic vocals that imitate real artists. This paper examines the legal and technical dimensions of AI-based music creation (e.g., Google Gemini's music tools) under U.S. copyright law. We analyze whether a user who inputs one artist's protected lyrics into a GenAI system, directs it to use another artist's voice or style, publishes the resulting song, and monetizes it violates 17 U.S.C. Section 106's exclusive rights [3]. The analysis integrates Title 17 doctrine (rights of reproduction, derivative works, distribution), 17 U.S.C. Section 114's narrow sound recording protection [4], and the new voice-cloning laws emerging at the state level [20]. We argue that unauthorized lyric copying poses a high risk of infringement of the musical composition, whereas mere AI-generated voice imitation typically falls outside federal sound recording protection and instead implicates state publicity rights [12], [13]. Recent cases and legislation (Concord v. Anthropic [10]; Kadrey v. Meta [11]; Lehrman v. Lovo [12]; Tennessee's "ELVIS Act" [20]; UMG v. Uncharted Labs [14]; etc.) illustrate this split. We map AI technical components (prompt encoding, latent diffusion, neural vocoders, speaker embeddings) to legal risks and identify a regulatory gap: federal law robustly protects lyrics and melody but currently provides limited remedies for synthesized vocal likeness [22], [23]. The paper concludes with policy suggestions for clearer rules on AI music creation.

items.title: arXiv: Study examines generative AI's impact on creative industries, highlighting OpenAI's Sora model release, audience quality limits on AI content, UK copyright tensions, and major studios' AI strategies [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dream machine -- the next creative economy
items.summary:
A new study analyzes the transformation of creative industries driven by generative artificial intelligence, focusing on the December 2024 release of OpenAI's Sora video model as a pivotal moment. The research introduces the Human-AI Agency Continuum to map collaboration between humans and AI in creative work and identifies an audience-imposed "slop ceiling" limiting AI-generated content to 1-3% of platform streams despite making up 44% of uploads. It also highlights tensions revealed by the UK Government's 2025 consultation on AI and copyright, where most respondents opposed expanded AI training rights.

The study examines how major studios like Disney and Netflix are adapting to AI-augmented production pipelines, including Disney's $1 billion investment in OpenAI and Netflix's AI-native animation unit. It discusses challenges such as coordination breakdowns in creative supply chains and the emergence of new roles like prompt engineers and AI orchestrators. The authors propose four guiding principles for the industry's transition: transparency, consent, compensation, and human-centered design, supported by extensive quantitative analysis and supplementary materials.

The framework emphasizes epistemic mapping, offering a transparent, multi-dimensional view of how facts, interpretations, actors, and narratives interact over time. items.title: Study finds ChatGPT and Claude disagree on two-thirds of brand recommendations but converge on diagnosing failure modes 95% of the time across 7,763 joint failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Divergent Recommendations, Convergent Diagnoses: Cross-Provider Failure-Mode Convergence in AI Commercial Recommendation
items.summary:
A study analyzing product recommendations from ChatGPT and Claude found that the two AI providers disagree on brand recommendations about two-thirds of the time. However, when neither recommends a brand, they diagnose the failure mode—categorized as discoverability, compellingness, or positioning—in agreement 95% of the time across 7,763 joint failures. This high concordance in failure diagnosis increases as brand prominence decreases, reaching nearly complete agreement for less prominent regional brands.

The research highlights that ChatGPT and Claude use different generative approaches to make recommendations but converge on identifying why brands fail to be recommended, especially for the long tail of less prominent brands. Addressing these diagnosed failure modes improves brand visibility on both platforms, though strategies for category leaders require more provider-specific efforts focused on positioning and content.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A brand whose customers use both ChatGPT and Claude for product recommendations faces a strategic choice: a single optimization playbook, or one per provider? Across 215 commercially-framed prompts in four measurement batches, the two providers disagree on which brands they recommend roughly two-thirds of the time (cross-provider recommendation Jaccard 0.35, below the 0.50-0.61 same-prompt rerun baseline). The picks diverge. But when neither provider recommends a brand, we classify the failure into one of three modes -- discoverability (the brand never reaches the model), compellingness (it reaches the model but isn't mentioned), or positioning (it's mentioned but not recommended) -- and on 7,763 such joint failures, both providers diagnose the same failure mode 95.1% of the time (clustered 95% CI [94.3%, 95.7%]). Agreement rises monotonically with falling brand prominence, from 81% [78.2%, 84.0%] on category leaders to 99.6% [99.3%, 99.9%] on long-tail regional brands. The two providers reach their picks by measurably different generative routes -- Anthropic recommends from priors 43-52% of the time, OpenAI 8-29% -- but they converge on the failure diagnosis where it matters most for the long tail. Work that addresses the diagnosed failure mode lifts visibility on both providers; positioning - and content-level work for category leaders is more provider-specific.

items.title: Researchers propose Governance Inversion Hypothesis, arguing increased AI regulation may reduce organisational control by fragmenting authority and complicating oversight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Governance Inversion Hypothesis: Why More AI Regulation May Produce Less Organisational Control
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed the Governance Inversion Hypothesis (GIH) to address a paradox in AI governance: as regulatory measures increase and AI systems grow more complex, organizations may become more formally governed yet lose operational control over these systems. Contrary to the common belief that stronger regulation enhances accountability and oversight, the hypothesis suggests that expanding governance structures can fragment authority and complicate effective management of AI technologies.

The study draws on institutional theory and governance research to identify four mechanisms—authority fragmentation, symbolic governance expansion, externalization of control, and authority paralysis—that contribute to this erosion of control. As governance frameworks become more layered and procedural, organizations may face challenges in maintaining clear authority, technical insight, and the ability to intervene meaningfully in AI operations. The paper warns that the main risk in AI governance may not be a lack of regulation but the emergence of complex institutions that appear well-governed while actually diminishing their capacity to govern effectively.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26117v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper introduces the Governance Inversion Hypothesis (GIH) to explain a growing paradox in artificial intelligence (AI) governance: under conditions of increasing regulatory expansion and technological complexity, organisations may become more formally governed while simultaneously experiencing a decline in operational control over AI systems. Existing AI governance frameworks generally assume that stronger regulation improves accountability, oversight, and organisational control. This paper challenges that assumption by arguing that governance formalisation itself may contribute to the erosion of control in AI-intensive environments. Drawing on institutional theory, organisational governance research, accountability scholarship, and emerging AI governance literature, the paper develops a conceptual framework explaining how regulatory expansion may weaken operational authority through four interconnected mechanisms: authority fragmentation, symbolic governance expansion, externalisation of control, and authority paralysis. As governance systems become increasingly layered and procedurally dense, organisations may struggle to maintain coherent authority, technical visibility, escalation capability, and meaningful intervention power over opaque and externally mediated AI infrastructures. The paper extends institutional decoupling theory by introducing governance inversion as a structural condition in which governance expansion may actively undermine operational coherence rather than strengthen it. It concludes that the central risk in AI governance may not be the absence of governance structures, but the emergence of institutions that appear increasingly governed while progressively losing the capacity to govern effectively.

items.title: Researchers propose privacy-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for dynamic VR slice management in 6G SD-RAN, improving throughput by 34% and reducing privacy leakage by 85% in simulations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Privacy-Aware Agent Collaboration for Dynamic VR Slice Management in 6G SD-RAN
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a privacy-aware multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework to manage dynamic virtual reality (VR) slices in 6G Software-Defined Radio Access Networks (SD-RANs). This approach aims to optimize resource allocation for VR services, ensuring ultra-low latency and high throughput while safeguarding user data privacy. Simulations demonstrate that the framework improves throughput by up to 34%, reduces resource usage by 28%, and decreases privacy leakage by 85% compared to traditional methods.

The framework integrates mobility prediction and an information bottleneck encoder to enable effective and secure collaboration among cooperative agents managing end-to-end VR links. These innovations address the critical challenges of dynamic resource management in future 6G networks, supporting reliable and immersive VR experiences.

items.title: Researchers propose Geo-FairFed, a geometric fairness-aware routing system using hyperbolic graph neural networks and federated optimization to improve latency, energy use, and fairness in 6G and IoT edge networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometric Fairness-Aware Routing for Federated Edge Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Geo-FairFed, a routing system designed for emerging 6G and edge-intelligent networks that integrates hyperbolic graph neural networks with federated optimization to enhance latency, energy efficiency, and fairness across distributed edge devices. This approach models network topologies on a negatively curved manifold to capture hierarchical and asymmetric connections, while a global aggregator enforces fairness by minimizing routing loss and inequality based on Jain's fairness index. The system aims to balance performance equitably among nodes rather than focusing solely on aggregate metrics.

Theoretical analysis confirms convergence under certain curvature constraints and demonstrates that the fairness component leads to a Pareto-improving equilibrium in routing outcomes. Simulations on dynamic 6G-edge and IoT network topologies show that Geo-FairFed reduces average latency by 20%, cuts energy consumption by 17%, and improves fairness by up to 21% compared to existing federated and geometric routing protocols. These results suggest that embedding network topology in hyperbolic space and incorporating fairness into federated learning can significantly improve the efficiency and equity of large-scale network routing.

The study found that embedding topology in a hyperbolic manifold and including fairness into federated updates can significantly enhance the efficiency and equity of large-scale network routing.

items.originalTitle: Multiscale Exit-Join Dynamics: Tactical Consensus and Strategic Coalition Formation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multiscale model that integrates strategic decisions to exit or join coalitions with tactical consensus dynamics within those coalitions. This model generates coalition value through internal information aggregation and uses Aumann-Dreze payoffs, switching frictions, and acceptance rules to guide coalition restructuring. The framework features a fast-slow architecture where transferable coalition value arises from consensus processes, while coalition structures evolve based on incentive-driven exit and join behaviors.

The study characterizes equilibria involving both tactical and strategic factors, identifying conditions for unanimity, segregation, polarization, and cognitive barriers that maintain stable coalitions. It establishes fixed-point characterizations and existence results for the coupled dynamics. Numerical experiments reveal an instability-consensus paradox, where low or negative switching barriers can hinder strategic convergence but promote sufficient temporal mixing to achieve global tactical consensus.

These findings offer a unified perspective on coalition formation, consensus dynamics, information aggregation, and strategic stability in multi-agent systems, advancing understanding of how complex group behaviors emerge and persist.

items.title: Researchers introduce Video Memory Transformers for unsupervised real-time obstacle detection on autonomous agricultural rover, achieving state-of-the-art results on rapeseed dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unsupervised Memory-Enhanced Video Transformers: Obstacle Detection for Autonomous Agricultural Rover
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Video Memory Transformers for Anomaly Detection (VMTAD), an unsupervised method designed to detect obstacles in real-time for autonomous agricultural rovers. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional sensors like LiDAR, which cannot detect obstacles beneath plant canopies, and supervised camera-based methods that struggle with unseen obstacles. VMTAD uses a transformer architecture with a memory module that processes temporal context from previous frames, enabling effective detection in dynamic environments without requiring labeled data.

The system was tested on the 'Grillion' agricultural rover using a challenging rapeseed dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results with detection and segmentation AUC scores of 0.973 and 0.997, respectively. A lightweight version of VMTAD balances high accuracy with real-time inference speed of 14 milliseconds, which is crucial for ensuring the rover's operational safety by allowing timely obstacle detection and response.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While autonomous rovers have become indispensable to precision farming, achieving consistent operational safety remains a critical challenge. Conventional safety sensors, such as LiDAR, fail to detect obstacles positioned below the plant canopy, posing a significant risk. While camera-based supervised learning methods can detect common objects, they perform poorly when faced with obstacles that were not present in their training data. Actual unsupervised anomaly detection offers a solution by learning the normal visual patterns of an environment, but often fails for the dynamic scenes captured by a moving rover.\\ This paper introduces Video Memory Transformers for Anomaly Detection (VMTAD), a fully unsupervised method designed for real-time obstacle detection in dynamic agricultural scenes. VMTAD utilizes a transformer-driven architecture augmented with a dedicated memory module. This memory module leverages temporal context by processing encoded representations of preceding frames. This approach enables the system to effectively address the dynamic context caused by the robot's movement. The model is trained using only images that represent normal operation, requiring no data labels.\\ VMTAD was rigorously evaluated on the 'Grillion' agricultural rover. On a challenging rapeseed dataset, VMTAD achieved state-of-the-art performance, reaching a 0.973 detection and 0.997 segmentation Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. A lightweight variant provides an optimal balance of high accuracy and real-time inference (14 ms), which is critical for safety, as confirmed by our analysis of the rover's total stopping distance.

items.title: Researchers propose ARReST method to reduce redundancy in whole-slide image patching, achieving 3% to 60% storage savings while maintaining retrieval accuracy across 21 organs in TCGA dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reducing Redundancy in Whole-Slide Image Patching for Scalable Indexing and Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a new method designed to reduce redundancy in whole-slide image (WSI) patching for digital pathology. ARReST targets patches that contribute little to distinguishing between different tissue classes, pruning them to significantly decrease the number of patches indexed without compromising retrieval accuracy. This approach addresses the high storage costs associated with WSI indexing, which is critical for supporting retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows in clinical decision-making.

Testing on The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset, which includes images from 21 organs, demonstrated that ARReST can achieve storage savings ranging from 3% to 60% while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. By reducing unnecessary patch representations, ARReST lowers storage requirements and computational overhead, enabling faster similarity searches and more scalable, cost-effective indexing of large pathology image repositories. This method holds promise for enhancing the efficiency of next-generation clinical AI systems reliant on retrieval-driven workflows.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26157v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid growth of digital pathology has created an urgent need for efficient indexing and retrieval of whole slide images (WSIs). This need is intensified by emerging generative AI workflows, particularly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which require dependable similarity search to support high-stakes clinical decision-making. Yet the substantial cost of high-performance storage limits the scalability and accessibility of WSI indexing for many healthcare institutions. Consequently, methods that can reduce storage demands while preserving retrieval accuracy have become a critical research priority. We propose ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a principled oppositional framework that leverages redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes to markedly decrease the number of patches that must be indexed from each WSI. Instead of eliminating only within-class duplicates, ARReST identifies antithetical patches-those whose representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination-and prunes them from the searchable archive. This targeted reduction substantially compresses the index without sacrificing morphological diversity or retrieval fidelity. By minimizing superfluous patch representations, ARReST reduces storage footprint, lowers computational overhead, and accelerates similarity search across large pathology repositories. Extensive experiments on TCGA repository (The Cancer Genome Atlas with 21 organs) demonstrate that ARReST achieves significant index compression while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. The observed storage savings of 3% to 60% (14%$\pm$13%) can be reliably achieved without compromising retrieval performance for many organs. The proposed strategy enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing and is well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems.

items.title: Researchers propose LCG framework with Sparse Relational Attention for consistent long-context multi-image generation, introducing a large synthetic dataset with 600K sequences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LCG: Long-Context Consistent Image Generation with Sparse Relational Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Long-Context Generation (LCG), a new framework designed to improve consistency in multi-image text-to-image generation over extended sequences, which is crucial for applications like comics and storyboards. LCG uses Sparse Relational Attention (SRA) to efficiently focus on key features across long visual contexts and employs a Routing Consistency Constraint (RCC) to maintain semantic alignment and reduce appearance drift, even in complex scenes with multiple characters. To support this work, the team created the Long-Context Consistency Dataset (LCCD), a large synthetic dataset with 600,000 training sequences and 1,000 test sequences, each containing 6 to 20 images.

Experiments demonstrate that LCG outperforms existing methods in maintaining prompt alignment and character consistency across long image sequences. The introduction of SRA and RCC mechanisms enables scalable and coherent generation, addressing challenges in long-context multi-image synthesis and advancing the quality of visual narrative generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26171v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent image generation models achieve impressive quality in single-image synthesis, but often fail to maintain consistency across sequential outputs, as required in comics, storyboards, and visual narratives. We propose Long-Context Generation (LCG), a framework for long-context multi-image text-to-image generation, to improve consistency and scalability in long-context multi-image generation. LCG employs the Sparse Relational Attention (SRA) mechanism to selectively attend to core features across extended visual contexts, ensuring that the propagation of semantic and layout information remains computationally tractable. To enforce semantic alignment, we introduce the Routing Consistency Constraint (RCC), which leverages identity-aware masks to align structural patterns across generation branches, effectively mitigating drift in appearance even in complex multi-character scenes. To support training and evaluation in this setting, we construct the Long-Context Consistency Dataset (LCCD), a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising character-centric multi-image sequences spanning varied situational contexts. LCCD contains 600K training sequences and a separate 1K test set, with each sequence containing 6 to 20 images. The experiments demonstrate that LCG outperforms the compared baselines in prompt alignment and character consistency for long-context image generation, including multi-character scenes.

items.title: Researchers present CyberChainBench, a benchmark evaluating LLM-based AI agents on smart contract security using 541 real-world exploits across 9 EVM chains with detection, exploitation, and patching tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?
items.summary: Researchers have introduced CyberChainBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM)-based AI agents on smart contract security. The benchmark covers three key tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis, using data from 541 real-world exploits across nine Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) chains. CyberChainBench enables end-to-end on-chain evaluation by allowing agents to interact with historical blockchain states in isolated environments, assessing their ability to identify vulnerabilities, generate exploits, and create effective patches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present CyberChainBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security across three complementary tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis. Built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains, the benchmark provides end-to-end on-chain evaluation where agents interact with historical blockchain state through isolated evaluation environments orchestrated by Harbor, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. Each case is anchored to a specific block and includes structured ground truth covering vulnerability type, localization, and attacker profit. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. We define a five-type vulnerability taxonomy and evaluate multiple agent--model configurations. Results reveal a clear difficulty gradient: the best configuration scores 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, but only 23.4% on patching, with the top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizing \$57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.

items.title: Lacuna uses large language models to create a machine learning research map with summaries, concepts, and proposals, outperforming OpenScholar in retrieval and report quality benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lacuna: A Research Map for Machine Learning
items.summary:
Lacuna is a research mapping tool for machine learning that leverages large language models to convert academic papers and metadata into structured markdown summaries, concept elements, research directions, and proposals, all linked to their original sources. It offers web, markdown, and MCP interfaces and demonstrates superior performance compared to OpenScholar, particularly in retrieval tasks such as LitSearch.

Evaluations across multiple benchmarks show Lacuna's enhanced capabilities, with its Deep Research agent achieving higher citation precision and report quality scores than competing systems like GPT-Researcher. This advancement highlights Lacuna's potential to improve the organization and accessibility of machine learning research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lacuna is a research map for machine learning that uses LLMs to turn papers and scholarly metadata into markdown summaries, concept elements, research directions, and research proposals. Each item keeps links to the primary source records and papers that support it. We release the map with web, markdown, and MCP interfaces. Across LitSearch, Multi-XScience-CS/ML, and ScholarQA-CS-ML, Lacuna outperforms OpenScholar with the strongest gains on LitSearch retrieval (Recall@10 0.538 vs. 0.424 for OpenScholar v3). We also evaluate Lacuna Deep Research, a multi-stage report agent over the map, on 25 ReportBench-ML survey tasks: Lacuna Deep Research reaches 0.052 citation F1, 0.339 citation precision, 99 expert-reference hits, and 7.82/10 RACE report quality, while GPT-Researcher reaches 0.039 F1, 0.290 precision, 72 hits, and 5.24/10 RACE.

items.originalTitle: A multi-task spatiotemporal deep neural network for predicting penetration depth and morphology in laser welding
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-task spatiotemporal deep neural network that predicts penetration depth, penetration state, and weld seam morphology in laser welding with high accuracy. Using weld pool images captured by a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor camera during the welding process, the model combines spatial and temporal features with welding parameters through convolutional neural networks and state space models. This approach enables efficient extraction and processing of spatial-temporal information for quality assessment.

The study also introduces a reliable dataset construction method to improve the model's robustness and generalization. Validation results show the model achieves 99.35% accuracy in predicting penetration state, a penetration depth error of 1.79 millimeters, and 95.65% accuracy in reconstructing the weld cross-section. These findings offer new methodologies for in-situ quality control in laser penetration welding systems.
